papers.title: Holographically motivated Hubble-running dark energy: Phantom-divide crossing in VCDM and observational constraints
papers.authors: Antonio De Felice, Burin Gumjudpai, Shinji Tsujikawa, Jack Zidich
papers.abstract: Motivated by power-law dependences on the expansion scale in holographic dark-energy constructions, we study the Hubble-running equation of state $w_{\rm DE}=w_0(H/H_0)^q$ (HoloEoS), where $H$ is the Hubble expansion rate, $H_0$ and $w_0$ are the present values of $H$ and $w_{\rm DE}$, and $q$ is a constant dimensionless exponent controlling the running. We embed this history in VCDM, a type-II minimally modified gravity theory that propagates only the two tensor modes of general relativity. For regular expanding histories with standard matter, we reconstruct the potential $V(\phi)$ of its nondynamical auxiliary scalar field, providing a Lagrangian description of both the homogeneous background and cosmological perturbations. This framework allows HoloEoS to realize a smooth late-time crossing of the phantom divide $w_{\rm DE}=-1$. We confront this VCDM realization with SPT, Planck, and ACT CMB data, updated DESI DR2 distances, and optionally DESY5 supernovae with Dovekie recalibration, comparing it with $\Lambda$CDM and the Chevallier--Polarski--Linder parameterization embedded in the same gravitational framework (CPL-VCDM). For the full data combination, the posterior medians and central $68\%$ credible intervals are $w_0=-0.881^{+0.040}_{-0.038}$ and $q=0.453^{+0.143}_{-0.133}$, with a crossing redshift $z_\times=0.476^{+0.106}_{-0.081}$ conditional on $0<z_\times<6$. For this data combination, physical-likelihood optimization by Metropolis--Hastings (MH) simulated annealing gives Akaike information criterion differences of $\Delta\mathrm{AIC}\simeq-3.40$ for HoloEoS and $-4.10$ for CPL-VCDM relative to $\Lambda$CDM. Thus, a Hubble-scale-motivated dark-energy history realized within a specified gravitational theory achieves fitting performance comparable to CPL-VCDM while naturally allowing phantom-divide crossing.

conclusions: Joint fits to CMB (Planck, ACT, SPT), DESI DR2 BAO, and DES Y5 supernovae constrain the HoloEoS parameters to $w_0 = -0.881^{+0.040}_{-0.038}$ and $q = 0.453^{+0.143}_{-0.133}$, corresponding to a transition from a phantom-like past ($w_{\rm DE} < -1$) to a quintessence-like present ($w_{\rm DE} > -1$) across the phantom divide at redshift $z_\times = 0.476^{+0.106}_{-0.081}$.

Including the DES Y5 supernova data improves the best-fit physical $\chi^2$ relative to flat $\Lambda$CDM by $\Delta\chi^2 \simeq -7.40$ ($\Delta\mathrm{AIC} \simeq -3.40$), matching the statistical preference of the standard $w_0 w_a$ parametrization in VCDM ($\Delta\mathrm{AIC} \simeq -4.10$), whereas without supernovae $\Lambda$CDM remains slightly favored by AIC ($\Delta\mathrm{AIC} = +1.76$).

Realizing the phantom-divide crossing within VCDM keeps linear gravitational perturbations completely regular—corresponding simply to an inflection point ($V_{,\phi\phi}=0$) in the reconstructed auxiliary potential—without introducing extra propagating scalar modes or alleviating the $H_0$ and $S_8$ tensions (slightly lowering $H_0$ and raising $S_8$ relative to $\Lambda$CDM).

Motivated by holographic dark energy (which links vacuum energy density to cosmological horizon scales), the authors propose a two-parameter "Hubble-running" equation of state, $w_{\rm DE} = w_0(H/H_0)^q$ (HoloEoS), and embed it into VCDM, a type-II minimally modified gravity theory. By reconstructing the potential $V(\phi)$ of a non-dynamical auxiliary scalar field in VCDM, they generate the exact HoloEoS background expansion while propagating only the two standard tensor modes of General Relativity, completely avoiding any unstable scalar perturbations across $w_{\rm DE} = -1$. Implementing this self-consistent background and linear perturbation system into CLASS, they confront the model with Planck, ACT, and SPT CMB data, DESI DR2 BAO, and DES Y5 supernovae, demonstrating that a physically stable, Hubble-scale-driven dark energy history fits current observations just as well as the standard $w_0 w_a$ (CPL) parametrization.

papers.title: Full-shape analysis of the Lyman-alpha forest power spectrum and bispectrum: validation on simulations
papers.authors: Roger de Belsunce, James M. Sullivan, Mikhail M. Ivanov
papers.abstract: The Lyman-$\alpha$ (LyA) forest of neutral hydrogen provides a large-volume, high-resolution map of cosmological fluctuations from optical spectra at high redshift. To extract more information from the currently observing Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI), we derive an effective field theory (EFT) model for joint full-shape analyses of the LyA forest data. It combines the one-loop power spectrum of the LyA forest (FF), and of its cross-correlation with dark-matter halos, used as proxies for high-redshift quasars (FQ), with the tree-level bispectrum of the LyA forest (FFF). Importantly, the bispectrum breaks the LyA-specific degeneracy between the mean flux and the amplitude of the power spectrum. We validate our theory framework on idealized large-volume LyA forest mocks painted onto the AbacusSummit N-body simulation suite at redshift z=2.5. Fitting scales up to $k_\mathrm{max}^{FF\,(FQ)}=0.6\,(0.3)\,h\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}$ in the power spectrum and $k_\mathrm{max}^{FFF}=0.1\,h\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}$ in the bispectrum, our full-shape analysis yields unbiased constraints on the cosmological parameters in simulations. For a fully sampled flux field in a simulated volume of $V=8\,h^{-3}\,{\rm Gpc}^3$, we measure the Hubble constant, $H_0$, to $0.6\%$, the matter density, $\Omega_{\rm m}$, to $1.6\%$ and the amplitude of matter clustering, $\sigma_8$, to $3.5\%$. Adding the bispectrum improves the constraints on $\sigma_8$ by $28\%$. We also demonstrate that the inclusion of the quasar one-loop power spectrum (QQ) and tree-level bispectrum (QQQ) further improves cosmological constraints by $\approx 35\%$ using $k_\mathrm{max}^{QQ,\,(QQQ)}=0.2,\,(0.08)\,h\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}$. Our theory framework enables full-shape analyses of high-redshift data from DESI and its successor DESI-II, enhancing knowledge of the growth of structure of the Universe during matter-domination.

conclusions: The joint EFT model recovers unbiased cosmological constraints on idealized $V = 8\,h^{-3}\,\mathrm{Gpc}^3$ simulation volumes up to $k_{\max} = 0.6\,(0.3)\,h\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}$ for the $FF$ ($FQ$) power spectra and $k_{\max} = 0.1\,h\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}$ for the $FFF$ bispectrum, measuring $H_0$ to $0.6\%$, $\Omega_{\rm m}$ to $1.6\%$, and $\sigma_8$ to $3.5\%$.

Including the tree-level Ly-$\alpha$ bispectrum ($FFF$) alongside the power spectra breaks key degeneracies with quadratic bias parameters—tightening $b_2$, $b_{\mathcal{G}_2}$, and $b_1$ by $72\%$, $67\%$, and $32\%$—which directly improves the $\sigma_8$ constraint by $28\%$ ($\sigma_8 = 0.809 \pm 0.028$).

Adding the quasar auto-power spectrum ($P_{QQ}$) to the standard $FF+FQ$ baseline actually yields stronger amplitude gains ($\approx 43\%$ on $\sigma_8$) than adding the Ly-$\alpha$ bispectrum alone, because quasars lack the unconstrained velocity-gradient bias $b_\eta$ and thus directly measure $f\sigma_8$.

Combining the full set of two- and three-point statistics ($FF + FQ + P_{QQ} + FFF + B_{QQQ}$) tightens constraints on $\ln(10^{10}A_s)$, $\sigma_8$, and $\Omega_{\rm m}$ by $55\%$, $57\%$, and $17\%$ respectively over the baseline $FF+FQ$ power-spectrum analysis.

ai.summary: The Lyman-$\alpha$ (Ly-$\alpha$) forest—the dense series of absorption lines in background quasar spectra caused by neutral hydrogen in the intergalactic medium—maps large-scale structure at high redshifts ($2 \lesssim z \lesssim 4$) during the matter-dominated era, complementing lower-redshift galaxy surveys. However, extracting full cosmological information from the 3D Ly-$\alpha$ power spectrum alone is limited by a strong degeneracy between the overall matter clustering amplitude ($\sigma_8$) and unknown bias parameters, especially the line-of-sight velocity gradient bias ($b_\eta$) that arises because the nonlinear mapping from gas density to transmitted flux does not conserve "tracer number." In this paper, the authors develop a unified Effective Field Theory of Large-Scale Structure (EFTofLSS) framework that combines the one-loop Ly-$\alpha$ auto-power spectrum ($FF$) and Ly-$\alpha$–quasar cross-power spectrum ($FQ$) with the tree-level 3D Ly-$\alpha$ bispectrum ($FFF$, the three-point Fourier-space statistic capturing non-Gaussian triangle configurations). They validate this pipeline on idealized, fully sampled synthetic Ly-$\alpha$ mocks painted onto the AbacusSummit $N$-body simulation suite at $z=2.5$ using the fluctuating Gunn–Peterson approximation. This work demonstrates that joint full-shape analyses of 3D Ly-$\alpha$ and quasar two- and three-point statistics can break key bias degeneracies and tightly constrain structure growth at high redshift with DESI and DESI-II.

papers.abstract: Euclid is expected to discover ~$10^5$ galaxy-galaxy strong gravitational lenses across ~14,000deg$^2$, requiring automated searches with high completeness and low false-positive rates. Despite advances in deep learning, the effects of training-set composition, image representation, and preprocessing on survey-scale detection remain poorly understood. We present an ablation study of the convolutional neural network used in the ECLIPSE strong-lens detection pipeline, evaluating different training configurations on a fixed test set. Using simulated and real Euclid data, we compare VIS-only and pseudo-RGB representations, FITS and JPEG formats, training-set composition, hard-negative selection, and multi-stage training. We also assess ensembling on ~67 million DR1 cutouts. Training-set composition and strategy strongly affect high-Recall performance. Omitting simulation based pre-training reduces high-Recall weighted average Precision by 83.7% for VIS-only and 74.5% for pseudo-RGB models. Negative-sample selection also substantially affects performance, while FITS yields modest gains over JPEG at high Recall (~2-5%). On DR1, the logit-mean ensemble improves average Precision by 28.0% and 39.9% over the individual VIS-only and pseudo-RGB models. Among ~70,000 candidates selected for visual inspection, it recovers 11,256 unique grade A (secure) and B (probable) lenses, compared with 9650 and 10,395 for the individual models. The branches show complementary ranking preferences, particularly for lenses benefiting from near-infrared information. Careful training-set design, realistic negatives, and multi-band ensembling improve survey-scale searches. Our final ensemble achieves ~80% Recall at the operational selection threshold, outperforming ablation models with higher global classification metrics and highlighting the need to optimise performance for realistic survey conditions.[Abridged]

conclusions: Two-stage training is critical for completeness: omitting simulation-based pre-training (Stage 0) before fine-tuning on real observations reduces high-Recall weighted average precision by $83.7\%$ for VIS-only and $74.5\%$ for pseudo-RGB models, because simulations expose the network to a much broader diversity of lens geometries than existing real catalogues.

Ensembling optical and near-infrared representations substantially boosts discovery yield: on the full $\sim 67$ million DR1 cutout sample, a logit-mean ensemble improves average precision by $28.0\%$ (over VIS-only) and $39.9\%$ (over pseudo-RGB), recovering $11\,256$ unique grade A/B lenses ($\sim 79.1\%$ of known lenses in the DR1 sample) within a visual-inspection budget of $68\,021$ candidates—$1606$ more lenses than VIS-only alone.

Curating "hard negatives" (objects like ring galaxies or spirals that mimic lensing) must be carefully staged: introducing the hardest contaminants only during Stage 1 fine-tuning on real data yields the best high-Recall performance, whereas adding poorly balanced negative subcategories degrades precision in the high-completeness regime by $60\%$–$78\%$.

Training on uncompressed FITS images rather than dynamic-range-compressed JPEGs provides a modest but consistent $2\%$–$5\%$ gain in high-Recall precision ($5.2\%$ for the ensemble), showing that preserving raw photometric dynamic range helps but is secondary to training-set design and multi-band ensembling.

ai.summary: Strong galaxy-galaxy gravitational lensing—where a foreground galaxy bends light from a background galaxy into multiple images or Einstein rings—is a powerful probe of dark matter Halo profiles and time-delay cosmography, and Euclid is expected to find $\sim 10^5$ such systems across its $14\,000\,\mathrm{deg}^2$ survey. Because true lenses are outnumbered roughly a thousand to one by ordinary galaxies and lookalike "impostors" (such as spiral arms or ring galaxies), automated deep-learning classifiers must be tuned not just for average accuracy, but specifically to rank true lenses at the very top of a manageable visual-inspection list (the high-recall, high-purity regime). In this paper, the Euclid Collaboration performs a systematic ablation study on a ConvNeXt-Base convolutional neural network within the ECLIPSE strong-lens detection pipeline, testing how image formats (full-dynamic-range FITS vs. compressed JPEG), spectral bands (high-resolution optical VIS-only vs. multi-band optical + near-infrared "pseudo-RGB"), two-stage training (pre-training on simulations before fine-tuning on real data), and the curation of "hard negative" non-lenses impact performance across $\sim 67$ million galaxy cutouts from Euclid Data Release 1 (DR1). This work demonstrates that data curation and multi-band ensembling matter far more than minor preprocessing tweaks, establishing a practical blueprint for discovering tens of thousands of strong lenses in wide-field surveys.

papers.title: The Full-Shape Analysis of the Fading Dark Sector Model
papers.authors: Georges Obied, Cumrun Vafa, David H. Wu
papers.abstract: We analyze the Fading Dark Sector (FDS) model, which is motivated by string theory and in which the fading of the dark sector is driven by a scalar field. The model is specified by two $O(1)$ numbers $(c,c')$ that parametrize the logarithmic derivatives of the dark energy and dark matter densities with respect to the field in Planck units. In previous work, we showed that this model provides a good fit to the DESI BAO, CMB, and SN datasets. Here, we extend that analysis to include the DESI DR1 full-shape galaxy power spectrum, which adds information about the time evolution of cosmic structure and provides an independent consistency check of the FDS model. We find that, when the DESI DR1 full-shape data are combined with CMB+DESI DR2 BAO+DES-Dovekie, the FDS model outperforms the Chevallier-Polarski-Linder (CPL) $w_0$-$w_a$ parameterization by $\Delta \chi^2_{\rm MAP}=-4$ at equal parameter count and is preferred over $\Lambda$CDM at $4.1\sigma$. The inferred values of $(c,c')$ with the full-shape data are unchanged from our previous analysis, so this improvement indicates that FDS makes a prediction for the growth of structure that captures the observed growth history better than the $w_0$-$w_a$ parameterization.

conclusions: Combining Planck CMB, DESI DR2 BAO, DESI DR1 full-shape clustering, and DES-Dovekie SNe Ia yields a $4.1\sigma$ preference for the Fading Dark Sector (FDS) model over $\Lambda$CDM ($\Delta\chi^2_{\rm MAP} = -20.1$), outperforming the two-parameter $w_0w_a$ model by $\Delta\chi^2_{\rm MAP} = -4.0$ at equal parameter count.

Adding full-shape growth data leaves the inferred scalar couplings completely consistent with background-only fits at $c = -0.82^{+0.11}_{-0.15}$ (dark energy slope) and $c' = 0.053^{+0.007}_{-0.006}$ (dark matter slope), while shrinking the error bar on $c$ by a factor of $1.3\text{--}1.7$.

The best-fit $c' \approx 0.05$ implies a long-range attractive fifth force between dark matter particles of strength $2c'^2 \approx 0.5\%$ relative to standard gravity; this boosts early-time clustering ($\sigma_8 = 0.829 \pm 0.008$) while the decaying dark matter mass suppresses the late-time growth rate ($\gamma_{\rm eff} \approx 0.57$ vs. $0.55$ in $\Lambda$CDM), matching the $f\sigma_8$ trend favored by DESI full-shape data.

Even without supernova data (using only CMB + DESI DR2 BAO + DESI DR1 full-shape), the FDS model is preferred over $\Lambda$CDM at $3.4\sigma$ and improves upon $w_0w_a$ by $\Delta\chi^2_{\rm MAP} \approx -3.5$, showing that background distances and structure growth mutually reinforce each other in FDS whereas they pull in slightly different directions in $w_0w_a$.

However, background distances alone are degenerate across many physical theories, whereas the "full shape" (FS) of the galaxy power spectrum—which captures redshift-space distortions, the Alcock-Paczynski effect, and the broadband power spectrum shape—directly tests how cosmic structure grows over time. In this paper, the authors test the string-theory-motivated Fading Dark Sector (FDS) model, in which a rolling scalar field $\phi$ exponentially modulates both the dark energy potential ($V \propto e^{-c\phi}$) and dark matter particle mass ($m_{\rm DM} \propto e^{-c'\phi}$), introducing both a modified Hubble friction and a dark-sector fifth force $G_{\rm eff} = G_N(1 + 2c'^2)$ on sub-horizon scales. Crucially, because $(c, c')$ simultaneously fix the background expansion and perturbation evolution without extra free parameters, FDS makes a rigid prediction for structure growth that fits the combined datasets significantly better than both $\Lambda$CDM and $w_0w_a$.

papers.title: Augmenting Galaxy Catalogues using Machine Learning in the FLAMINGO Simulations
papers.authors: Elliot Scott, Marika Asgari, Joop Schaye, Matthieu Schaller, Markus Michael Rau
papers.abstract: Hydrodynamic simulations are instrumental in the analysis of observations such as galaxy clustering used for the estimation of cosmological parameters. However, for these purposes, the simulations need both a large box size and high resolution, which is computationally prohibitive. In this work we use the connection between galaxies and their host dark matter halos to populate dark-matter-only simulations, using data from the FLAMINGO simulations suite. We employ the Extremely Randomized Trees algorithm to model the connection between the mass profile, history and environment of dark matter halos and the probability distribution of the stellar mass of the galaxy contained in the halo. We use halos matched between a dark-matter-only simulation and the corresponding hydrodynamical simulation to train a model for centrals. For satellites, we employ a Gaussian Processes emulator that simultaneously optimises the hyperparameters of a model and selects for the dark matter features that are predictive of the stellar mass while being insensitive to the differences between the hydrodynamic and dark-matter-only simulations, then train a model on only these features. We then apply these models to produce a new galaxy catalogue for the 2.8 Gpc FLAMINGO-10k dark-matter-only simulation as a product of this work. We demonstrate that this catalogue reproduces the statistics of the galaxy-halo connection predicted by the smaller volume hydrodynamical simulation on which the model was trained, including the stellar mass function, stellar mass-dark matter mass relation, 2-point correlation functions and correlations between stellar mass and dark matter concentration, half mass radius and dark matter mass within 3 Mpc.

conclusions: By predicting binned stellar mass probability distributions with Extremely Randomized Trees rather than single point estimates, the pipeline accurately captures both the median and the intrinsic scatter (16th and 84th percentiles) of the stellar mass–halo mass relation across a wide mass range (with deviations up to $0.25\,\mathrm{dex}$ only below $M_{\mathrm{DM}} \sim 10^{12}\,M_\odot$, or $\sim 1000$ particles).

Training purely on hydrodynamical halo features (`HYDRO-opt`) fails when applied to DMO simulations because baryonic feedback alters internal halo properties (such as $V_{\mathrm{DM,peak}}$); using matched central halos and GP-selected feedback-insensitive features for satellites (`DMO-opt`) reproduces the target hydrodynamical stellar mass function to well within its $0.2\,\mathrm{dex}$ observational calibration uncertainty.

The resulting synthetic galaxy catalogue for the flagship $2.8\,\mathrm{Gpc}$ `FLAMINGO-10k` DMO run accurately recovers secondary environmental and structural correlations (such as halo concentration $c_{\mathrm{200c}}$, half-mass radius, and dark matter mass within $3\,\mathrm{Mpc}$) as well as galaxy two-point correlation functions across four stellar mass bins.

A much cheaper alternative is to run a huge dark-matter-only (DMO) $N$-body simulation and "paint" galaxies onto its dark matter halos by learning the galaxy–halo connection from a smaller hydrodynamical run. In this paper, the authors train Extremely Randomized Trees (an ensemble decision-tree classifier) on the $1\,\mathrm{Gpc}$ high-resolution FLAMINGO hydrodynamical simulation and its matched DMO counterpart to predict the full probability distribution of a galaxy's stellar mass from its host halo's mass profile, assembly history, and environment. Because satellite subhalos cannot be cleanly matched particle-by-particle between hydro and DMO runs, they use a Gaussian Process emulator to optimize hyperparameters and select only the 6 dark matter features that are insensitive to baryonic feedback Differences, then apply the trained models to populate the massive $2.8\,\mathrm{Gpc}$ `FLAMINGO-10k` DMO simulation with realistic central and satellite galaxies.

papers.title: Multipoles in the IllustrisTNG simulation galaxies and implications for Strong Gravitational Lens modelling in Time-delay Cosmography
papers.authors: Abdullah Al Zaif, Suhail Dhawan, Vasily Belokurov, Erin E. Hayes
papers.abstract: Time-delay cosmography is a powerful independent probe of the Hubble constant ($H_0$), yet reaching the sub-2$\%$ precision required to resolve the Hubble tension demands a rigorous treatment of mass model systematics. We use realistic massive elliptical galaxies from the IllustrisTNG hydrodynamic simulation suite to characterise higher-order angular mass complexity in the form of multipoles ($m=1,3,4$) and quantify their impact on $H_0$ inference. We find that these multipole perturbations are common and emergent features of galaxy assembly; in 51$\%$ of our total samples ($54\%$ TNG100-1 galaxies and $85\%$ for TNG50-1 galaxies), the addition of multipole terms to a standard elliptical power-law model is preferred by the Bayesian Information Criterion. Ignoring these structures in lens modelling introduces systematic biases in $H_0$: for perturbations of $\sim2\%$, the biases are of the order of 1--2$\%$ for $m=1$, 4--5$\%$ for $m=3$, and 3--6$\%$ for $m=4$ multipole. While the $m=4$ (boxy/discyness) mode induces a predictable directional bias, odd-order modes ($m=1,3$) introduce significant stochastic scatter. We demonstrate a degeneracy where unmodelled internal multipoles can be effectively absorbed by the external shear component. This combined with low signal-to-noise observations can create ``hidden biases'' where formally perfect fits to imaging data ($\chi_\nu^2 \approx 1$) could harbour significant cosmological errors. Our results provide an astrophysical basis for multipole priors and highlight the necessity of moving beyond rigid parametric models to achieve high-accuracy cosmography in the era of \textit{Euclid} and LSST.

conclusions: Higher-order angular multipoles ($m=1, 3, 4$) are common emergent features of galaxy assembly: adding multipole terms to a standard Elliptical Power Law (EPL) mass profile is statistically preferred (via the Bayesian Information Criterion) in $54\%$ of TNG100-1 and $85\%$ of higher-resolution TNG50-1 massive elliptical galaxies.

Ignoring typical $\sim 2\%$ multipole perturbations during lens modelling biases the inferred $H_0$ by $1\text{--}2\%$ for $m=1$, $4\text{--}5\%$ for $m=3$, and $3\text{--}6\%$ for $m=4$ in individual systems—exceeding the $<2\%$ total error budget needed to resolve the Hubble tension.

Fourth-order ($m=4$) perturbations cause a predictable directional bias (discy $a_4 > 0$ lenses systematically underestimate $H_0$, while boxy $a_4 < 0$ lenses overestimate it), whereas odd-order modes ($m=1, 3$) driven by mergers and companions inject substantial stochastic scatter into $H_0$ constraints.

Standard EPL + external shear models can absorb unmodelled internal multipoles (especially $m=3, 4$) into a spurious effective external shear; in lower signal-to-noise imaging, this produces "hidden biases" where image residuals look statistically perfect ($\chi_\nu^2 \approx 1$) despite carrying percent-level errors in $H_0$.

ai.summary: Time-delay cosmography measures the Hubble constant ($H_0$) independently of the local distance ladder and the CMB by tracking the arrival-time differences between multiple images of a strongly lensed background transient (like a supernova), which depend on the gravitational potential of the foreground lens galaxy. Standard analyses typically model the projected mass density of the lensing elliptical galaxy as a simple Elliptical Power Law (EPL) plus an external tidal shear, assuming pure elliptical symmetry and neglecting higher-order angular distortions ("multipoles") such as lopsidedness ($m=1$), triangularity ($m=3$), and boxy/discy shapes ($m=4$). In this work, the authors extract nearly 600 realistic massive elliptical galaxies from the IllustrisTNG magnetohydrodynamic simulations (TNG100-1 and TNG50-1), project their 3D dark matter and baryonic distributions into 2D lensing convergence maps, and test how unmodelled multipole structures impact $H_0$ inference in mock strong-lensing systems. Understanding and placing astrophysical priors on these internal mass asymmetries is critical because achieving a $<2\%$ uncertainty on $H_0$ to weigh in on the Hubble tension requires eliminating subtle lens-modelling systematics ahead of large strong-lens samples from Euclid and LSST.

papers.title: Note on quantum optimal measurements of CMB spectral distortions
papers.authors: Roshni Singh, Jacques Delabrouille, Daniel Carney
papers.abstract: As quantum sensing techniques continue to push the frontier of detection of ultra-weak signals, one may wonder if a sophisticated quantum strategy could be used to enable measurement of spectral distortions in the cosmic microwave background. Using quantum Fisher information techniques, we prove that the optimal strategy is simple frequency-binned intensity measurement. This proof strategy also enables us to provide numerical estimates for the information-theoretic minimum observation time required to observe the $\mu$- and $y$-distortions expected from $\Lambda$CDM cosmology. As case studies, we compare these results to the PIXIE and SPECTER mission concepts, and show that they are within a few orders of magnitude of this fundamental limit.

conclusions: Simple frequency-binned photon counting is proven to be the quantum-optimal strategy for measuring CMB spectral distortions, saturating the quantum Fisher information bound both with and without astrophysical foregrounds.

Because the CMB and foreground radiation fields lack phase coherence (their quantum density matrices are diagonal in the photon-number Fock basis), exotic quantum sensing strategies using entanglement or squeezing cannot improve sensitivity over ideal photon counting.

For a satellite mission with PIXIE/SPECTER-like geometry ($A\Omega \sim 20\,\mathrm{cm}^2\,\mathrm{sr}$ per horn, 10 horns, 10 GHz–2 THz in 1 GHz bins), the fundamental information-theoretic minimum observation time to detect the standard $\Lambda$CDM chemical potential distortion ($\mu \approx 2\times 10^{-8}$) in the presence of foregrounds is on the order of months.

Ideal frequency-binned photon counting is theoretically superior to Fourier Transform Spectroscopy (FTS), because FTS spreads photon shot noise across all frequency bins rather than isolating it within narrow bands.

With quantum sensing advancing rapidly in fields like gravitational-wave detection, the authors ask whether exotic quantum measurement strategies (such as entanglement-assisted or phase-sensitive detection) could help detect these ultra-weak CMB signals. By modeling the CMB radiation field and astrophysical foregrounds as quantum density matrices and computing the quantum Fisher information—which sets the absolute theoretical ceiling on how well parameters can be estimated from any quantum state—they prove that simple frequency-binned photon counting already saturates this fundamental quantum limit. They then apply the quantum Cramér-Rao bound to calculate the absolute minimum observation time needed to detect the standard $\Lambda$CDM $\mu$-distortion ($\mu \approx 2\times 10^{-8}$) and benchmark proposed missions like PIXIE and SPECTER against this ideal limit.

papers.title: Predicting Individual Dark Matter Halo Concentrations from Their Assembly Histories
papers.authors: Dao-Zhou Wang, Weipeng Lin, Weishan Zhu, Tian-Cheng Luan
papers.abstract: We present an empirical model for predicting concentration parameters of individual dark matter halos in cold and warm dark matter (WDM) cosmologies over z=0-5. Constructed using a large suite of cosmological N-body simulations, our model separately incorporates cosmic expansion (linear growth factor), mass scale (linear density fluctuations), halo mass assembly histories via the Extended Press-Schechter (EPS) scaled formation variable, plus a WDM damping term tied to the half-mode mass. It works for both virial and 200 $\rho_{crit}$ halo definitions. Across all tested cosmologies and redshifts, our global logarithmic fit gives concentration scatter ~0.09 dex for relaxed halos and ~0.09 to 0.10 dex for all halos. While relaxed halos maintain nearly constant scatter near 0.09 dex, the scatter of all halos at z>3 increases from 0.10 to 0.18 dex, revealing substantial violent-relaxation impacts on high-redshift halo structure. At fixed mass, concentration scatter is dominated by assembly history. We extract the scaled formation variable's probability distribution function (PDF) from merger trees and find departures from standard EPS theory. This PDF is narrower in WDM than LCDM due to suppressed small-scale perturbations and rapid, delayed monolithic collapse near the WDM truncation scale. Monte Carlo realizations with our formulae reproduce concentration distributions and match our prior peak-concentration model, whereas standard EPS underestimates concentrations from delayed-formation bias. Our framework offers a transparent, computationally lightweight tool to predict individual halo concentrations across diverse cosmological models.

conclusions: A compact 4-term power-law model decoupling $D(z)$, $\sigma(M)$, the EPS-scaled half-mass formation time $\omega_{\mathrm{f}}$, and the WDM half-mode cutoff scale $A_{\mathrm{hm}}$ predicts individual halo concentrations across $z=0\text{--}5$ for both virial ($\Delta_{\mathrm{vir}}$) and $200\rho_{\mathrm{crit}}$ definitions.

For dynamically relaxed halos, the model achieves a tight, nearly redshift-independent residual scatter of $\sigma_{\log c} \approx 0.088\text{--}0.089$ dex, showing that assembly history accounts for roughly 40%–50% of the total concentration variance at fixed halo mass.

For the unselected all-halo sample, scatter matches relaxed halos at $z=0$ ($\sim 0.094\text{--}0.096$ dex) but increases to $\sim 0.18$ dex at $z=5$ as the fraction of relaxed halos drops from 84% at $z=0$ to 34% at $z=5$ due to violent mergers and non-equilibrium accretion.

Reconstructing halo concentration distributions via Monte Carlo draws from the empirical merger-tree $P(\omega_{\mathrm{f}})$ accurately recovers population-level concentrations, whereas analytical EPS formation-time distributions systematically underpredict concentrations due to a delayed-formation bias (and fail to capture the narrower $\omega_{\mathrm{f}}$ distribution in WDM near the free-streaming cutoff).

This provides a fast, physically transparent recipe for populating large-scale survey mocks with realistic halo-to-halo structural scatter and assembly bias without needing to trace entire progenitor merger trees or run neural networks.

papers.title: Axion quintessence with a negative cosmological constant: Bayesian constraints from current cosmological data
papers.authors: Masroor C. Pookkillath, Gary Shiu, Shinji Tsujikawa
papers.abstract: We constrain canonical axion quintessence with a negative cosmological constant using DES Year 5 supernovae, DESI DR2 BAO, compressed CMB information, and geometry-corrected Gold-2017 growth data. We solve the background and linear-growth equations and sample with PolyChord. Our joint prior is logarithmic in the decay constant over $0.005\leq f/M_{\rm Pl}\leq10$ and uniform in the initial angle $\theta_i=\phi_i/f\in[0,\pi]$, conditioned on $\pi-\theta_i\geq H_{\rm inf}/(2\pi f)$ with $H_{\rm inf}=10^{13}$ GeV and reduced Planck mass $M_{\rm Pl}$. The broad-prior model favors recent thawing, with median $w_{{\rm DE},0}=-0.865^{+0.068}_{-0.053}$, $m_\phi\in[0.91,4.39]\times10^{-33}$ eV, and $f/M_{\rm Pl}\in[0.589,4.899]$ (central 68\% credible intervals). Bayes factors relative to flat $\Lambda$CDM are 0.70 and 30.1 for the normalized fluctuation-conditioned prior (Convention I) and its further conditioning on numerical acceptance (Convention II). Restricting $f\leq M_{\rm Pl}$ gives $f/M_{\rm Pl}\in[0.262,0.822]$ at 68\% credibility and Bayes factors 0.233 and 32.4. Relative to the zero-vacuum axion model, the broad-prior Bayes factors are 0.620 and 1.65, providing no compelling evidence for a negative cosmological constant. Local likelihood optimization gives an Akaike information criterion difference $\Delta{\rm AIC}\simeq-10.87$ for the zero-vacuum model relative to flat $\Lambda$CDM. For this model, assuming that the instanton generating $m_\phi^2f^2=\Lambda_{\rm UV}^4e^{-S_{\rm inst}}$ satisfies the axionic Weak Gravity Conjecture, the one-sided 95\% posterior lower limit on the minimum compatible coefficient $c_{\min}$ rises from 37 to 55 as the ultraviolet scale $\Lambda_{\rm UV}$ increases from $10^{-10}M_{\rm Pl}$ to $M_{\rm Pl}$, in tension with an order-one coefficient under these assumptions.

conclusions: The combined datasets favor a recently thawing dark energy evolution with a present-day equation of state $w_{{\rm DE},0} = -0.865^{+0.068}_{-0.053}$ (moving away from $-1$ at late times), an ultralight axion mass $m_\phi \in [0.91, 4.39] \times 10^{-33}\text{ eV}$ (comparable to $H_0$), and a decay constant $f/M_{\rm Pl} \in [0.589, 4.899]$ (68% credible intervals).

Adding a negative cosmological constant is statistically inconclusive compared to a pure zero-vacuum axion model (Bayes factors of $0.620$ and $1.65$ depending on prior normalization convention), meaning current data do not require an anti-de Sitter vacuum offset.

Bayesian model preference relative to flat $\Lambda$CDM depends heavily on prior volume effects: averaging over the full initial prior is inconclusive ($B = 0.70$), whereas conditioning the prior only on numerically viable expanding backgrounds yields moderate preference for the axion model ($B = 30.1$); meanwhile, local likelihood optimization favors the zero-vacuum axion model by $\Delta\text{AIC} \simeq -10.87$ (driven primarily by DES Y5 SNe and DESI DR2 BAO).

If the single nonperturbative instanton generating the axion cosine potential must also satisfy the axionic Weak Gravity Conjecture ($f S_{\rm inst} \le c_0 M_{\rm Pl}$), the posterior requires a minimum coefficient $c_{\min} \ge 37\text{--}55$ (at 95% confidence across UV scales $\Lambda_{\rm UV}/M_{\rm Pl} \in [10^{-10}, 1]$), placing single-instanton axion quintessence in strong tension with quantum gravity expectations ($c_0 \sim \mathcal{O}(1)$).

papers.abstract: The European Space Agency's Euclid mission has issued its first major data release(Data Release 1, DR1), providing a transformative view of the extragalactic sky through deep photometry and near-infrared slitless spectroscopy. This paper presents the Euclid DR1 spectroscopic data set and details the evolution of the spectroscopic processing function (SPE PF) pipeline, which is responsible for the automated analysis of 1-dimensional spectra acquired by the Near-Infrared Spectro-Photometer (NISP). The SPE PF pipeline workflow comprises spectroscopic classification, redshift determination, and the systematic measurement of spectral features. Emission line fluxes are derived using two independent methodologies: direct integration (DI) and Gaussian fitting (GF). For sources exhibiting broad H$\alpha$ profiles (velocity dispersion larger than $1500$ km s$^{-1}$), a dedicated `QSO mode' is implemented to robustly deconvolve nuclear and host galaxy components. The data set was validated by cross-matching Euclid results with external spectroscopic catalogues, specifically Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) DR1, and through an extensive visual inspection campaign of approximately 4000 sources within the Euclid Deep Field North (EDF-N). For high-quality samples selected in the EDF-N, we find a 98.5\% agreement between Euclid and DESI spectroscopic redshifts. This success rate increases to 98.9\% when incorporating pipeline probability and reliability estimators. (abridged)

conclusions: The Euclid DR1 spectroscopic release provides over 160 million redshifts in the Euclid Wide Survey (EWS) and 7.0 million in the Euclid Deep Fields (EDFs), including 2.7 million in the deepest field, EDF-North (EDF-N).

For emission-line galaxies, spectroscopic redshift measurements achieve high precision, with a median relative redshift error of $\sim 10^{-5}$ and a $1\sigma$ dispersion of $0.4 \times 10^{-3}$ (corresponding to velocity uncertainties of $\sim 120\text{ km s}^{-1}$) when validated against DESI DR1 and internal deep-to-wide comparisons.

In the EDF-N cosmological galaxy clustering sample, 75% of redshifts agree with DESI using Euclid spectroscopy alone, rising to 98%–98.9% when incorporating photometric redshifts and pipeline reliability estimators.
Using the deep survey as a reference, a tailored selection in the Euclid Wide Survey achieves the mission's target 80% sample purity within the cosmological redshift range using spectroscopy alone.

papers.title: General $δN$ formalism in Single Field Inflation and Graph Theory
papers.authors: Amin Nassiri-Rad, Hassan Firouzjahi
papers.abstract: We study higher order correlation functions in single field inflation using the $\delta N$ formalism and methods from graph theory. By representing connected tree level contributions as graphs, we systematically classify their independent topologies, momentum shapes and amplitudes. We show that the amplitudes of arbitrary trees factorize into products of primary amplitudes, providing a general framework for relations among higher order correlators, including the Suyama-Yamaguchi equality. As the number of external legs increases, the number of distinct tree topologies grows exponentially, whereas the number of algebraically distinct amplitude products grows considerably more slowly. As an application, we consider ultra-slow-roll inflation followed by a transition to a slow-roll attractor. For transitions without a potential step, we derive an explicit all-order expression for the vertex amplitudes and establish their positivity and dependence on the sharpness of the transition. When a potential step is included, we prove that all nonlinear vertex amplitudes remain positive for upward steps, whereas downward steps allow cancellations at specific parameter values. These cancellations can eliminate entire families of tree contributions, including configurations in which the leading local bispectrum and trispectrum vanish simultaneously while higher order correlations remain nonzero.

conclusions: Every connected tree-level $n$-point diagram has $n-1$ propagators, vertex degrees obeying $\sum_{v=1}^n d_v = 2(n-1)$, and a factorized amplitude $f_T = \prod_{v} a_{d_v}$ built from primary "star-tree" vertex amplitudes $a_d = N^{(d)}/(N')^d$—providing an all-order generalization of the tree-level Suyama–Yamaguchi equality ($T_{\rm NL} = F_{\rm NL}^2$).

While the number of distinct momentum shapes (non-isomorphic trees) grows exponentially with $n$, the number of distinct algebraic amplitudes (determined purely by the vertex degree sequence) grows much more slowly, meaning topologically distinct momentum configurations can share identical amplitudes.

For an inflationary phase transitioning from ultra-slow-roll to slow-roll ($h < 0$) across an upward or absent potential step ($0 < g \le 1$, where $g$ parametrizes the inflaton velocity change), all nonlinear vertex amplitudes $a_d$ ($d \ge 2$) and thus all connected tree-level $n$-point amplitudes are strictly positive to arbitrary order.

For downward potential steps ($g > 1$), competition between ultra-slow-roll evolution and the velocity boost across the step allows individual vertex amplitudes $a_d$ to change sign or vanish along specific curves in $(h, g)$ space, eliminating entire families of tree diagrams—for instance, making the local bispectrum ($f_{\rm NL}$) and trispectrum ($\tau_{\rm NL}, g_{\rm NL}$) vanish simultaneously while higher-order correlators remain nonzero.

As one moves to higher $n$-point functions, tracking all the possible Wick contractions and momentum shapes becomes combinatorially complex. In this paper, the authors map the perturbative $\delta N$ expansion in single-field inflation onto mathematical graph theory: each $\mathcal{R}_{\mathbf{k}_i}$ insertion is a vertex whose degree $d$ corresponds to the $d$-th derivative $N^{(d)}(\delta\phi)^d/d!$, and Gaussian contractions between vertices form edges in connected tree diagrams. They prove that the amplitude of any arbitrary tree diagram factorizes into a product of basic "star-tree" vertex amplitudes, and they apply this framework to an ultra-slow-roll (USR) inflationary phase—a regime where the inflaton potential is extremely flat and perturbations grow rapidly—transitioning into a standard slow-roll attractor, both with and without a sharp step in the potential. This provides a systematic way to classify all-order primordial correlators and reveals how specific inflationary transitions can selectively erase lower-order non-Gaussian signals while leaving higher-order ones intact.

papers.title: Cubic Galileon Gravity on Nonlinear Scales with \texttt{Hi-COLA} for LSST Year 1
papers.authors: C. M. A. Zanoletti, A. Sen Gupta, N. Ramachandra, T. Baker, B. Fiorini, K. Heitmann, D. Jones, C. D. Leonard, B. Li, N. Šarčević, for the LSST Dark Energy Science Collaboration
papers.abstract: Vera C. Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) is in a prime position to test Modified Gravity (MG) with Weak Lensing (WL) and Large Scale Structure (LSS). However, many nonlinear MG emulators in the literature enforce a $\Lambda$CDM background by design, missing where data suggest the most interesting deviations lie. We present an emulator for the 3D nonlinear matter power spectrum in Cubic Galileon gravity, a Horndeski theory with a single additional MG parameter, $f_\phi$, that modifies the background, growth, and lensing. Trained on \texttt{Hi-COLA} simulations with Gaussian Process Regression (GPR), the emulator achieves $\lesssim 2\%$ accuracy for $k \leq 1.2\ h\,\text{Mpc}^{-1}$ at the fiducial cosmology relative to \texttt{Hi-COLA}, and $\lesssim 5\%$ relative to full N-body \texttt{EFT-RAMSES} simulations. Additionally, conservative scale cuts excluding angular bins affected by baryonic physics enable unbiased parameter estimation in LSST Year 1 weak lensing and galaxy clustering ($3\times2$pt) forecasts, even when validated against simulated data based on higher-resolution N-body simulations. This demonstrates that, within a simplified LSST Y1 setup and the adopted scale cuts, \texttt{Hi-COLA}-based emulation is sufficient to develop inference infrastructure with Stage IV precision for Horndeski gravity models previously unmodeled on nonlinear scales.

conclusions: The GPR-based emulator reproduces `Hi-COLA` nonlinear matter power spectrum boosts to within $\sim 1\%$ near the center of the parameter space (for $k \lesssim 0.9\,h\,\text{Mpc}^{-1}$) and $\lesssim 2\%$ at the fiducial cosmology up to $k \leq 1.2\,h\,\text{Mpc}^{-1}$.

When benchmarked against a high-resolution `EFT-RAMSES` N-body simulation, the emulator and `Hi-COLA` boosts deviate by $\sim 5\%$ at $k \approx 1.2\,h\,\text{Mpc}^{-1}$, showing that the approximate COLA dynamics and spherical screening approximation dominate the small-scale error budget rather than emulator interpolation.

In simulated LSST Y1 $3\times 2$pt analyses against `EFT-RAMSES` mock data, optimistic scale cuts ($\ell^{\kappa\kappa} \leq 1500$) yield $\geq 2\sigma$ parameter biases, whereas applying conservative baryonic scale cuts (with $k_{\max} = 0.2\,h\,\text{Mpc}^{-1}$) fully recovers unbiased cosmological and modified gravity ($f_\phi$) posteriors.

Using paired phase-reversed initial conditions for each of the 50 Latin Hypercube nodes keeps finite-volume variance in the power spectrum boost within $2\%$ of a 10-realization ensemble average at only twice the computational cost of a single run.

This paper addresses that gap by focusing on Cubic Galileon gravity, a scalar-tensor theory within the general Horndeski framework that uses Vainshtein screening (where nonlinear scalar self-interactions suppress the fifth force in dense environments) and naturally alters both the background expansion and linear/nonlinear clustering via a single parameter $f_\phi$ (the fraction of dark energy density contributed by the scalar field today along a stable attractor "tracker" trajectory). The authors run a suite of 50 phase-reversed pairs of fast, approximate `Hi-COLA` simulations across a 5D parameter space ($\Omega_{m0}, n_s, A_s, h, f_\phi$) and use Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) to emulate the nonlinear matter power spectrum boost $B(k,z) = P_{\text{CuGal}}/P_{\Lambda\text{CDM}}$. papers.title: Distinguishing cosmologies with topological analysis of 21-cm hydrogen 2D brightness fields at Cosmic Dawn
papers.authors: Maksym Tsizh, Anton Rudakovskyi, Vitalii Tymchyshyn
papers.abstract: The 21-cm hydrogen line brightness field is a potentially valuable source of information about astrophysical parameters during the cosmological Dark Ages and the Epoch of Reionization. However, it can also be a source of observational data for cosmologists seeking to constrain cosmological parameters. While much of the effort has been focused on constraining parameters using information across a broad frequency range, most often with the power spectrum of inhomogeneities, we investigate whether a single frequency channel, corresponding to a single redshift slice, can distinguish between cosmological models. We utilize topological data analysis to evaluate the possibility of such constraints. In particular, we use cubical complexes to perform persistent homology analysis of the 21-cm line brightness field. We generate 21-cm brightness fields of different cosmologies with the 21cmFAST package and then select snapshots at several redshifts corresponding to the Epoch of Reionization. Our goal is to find the redshift that is most suitable for highlighting the diversity between scenarios within a certain range of cosmological parameters. To compare persistent pictures built on simulations of the brightness field, we use Wasserstein distance, computed between any two persistent diagrams. We find that observations of the 21-cm field near $z=10$ have the potential to distinguish between cosmological models with different values of the normalized Hubble parameter $h_0$, the spectral index of scalar matter perturbations $n_s$, the matter density parameter $\Omega_m$, and the matter fluctuation amplitude $\sigma_8$, even in the presence of instrumental thermal noise. We perform the PERMANOVA statistical test on the matrices of Wasserstein distances to confirm this hypothesis for all considered cosmological parameters.

conclusions: The topological separation between different $\Lambda$CDM parameter values peaks at $z \in [9.5, 10.5]$, yielding PERMANOVA $p$-values $< 0.005$ on clean maps for $\sim 2\sigma$ and $\sim 4\sigma$ shifts in $h_0$ ($\Delta = 0.02, 0.05$), $n_s$ ($0.005, 0.01$), $\Omega_m$ ($0.014, 0.028$), and $\sigma_8$ ($0.012, 0.024$). Physically, this $z \simeq 10$ sweet spot corresponds to when X-ray heating brings the mean intergalactic medium kinetic temperature close to the CMB temperature ($T_K \simeq T_{\rm CMB}$), producing a non-Gaussian field with both emission (heated regions) and absorption (cold voids) around a near-zero mean.

papers.title: Precise Deep-Learning Reconstruction of Galaxy Cluster Mass Maps and Substructures from Optical Observations

Conventional mass-mapping techniques rely predominantly on gravitational lensing and often produce smooth mass distributions based on analytical profiles, potentially missing important internal substructures. We trained deep learning models on realistic hydrodynamical simulations of galaxy clusters to infer their mass distributions from optical observations. We subsequently applied this framework to observations of real galaxy clusters obtained with the Hubble Space Telescope (HST) as part of the Cluster Lensing And Supernova survey with Hubble (CLASH) programme. The reconstructed mass maps successfully reproduce the overall shapes and radial mass profiles of the CLASH clusters, showing strong agreement with independent gravitational lensing measurements. Furthermore, the subhalo mass functions derived from the reconstructed maps exhibit power-law behaviour broadly consistent with predictions from numerical simulations. Our results demonstrate that combining optical imaging with deep learning provides a scalable and physically meaningful approach to mapping galaxy cluster mass distributions. This framework opens a new avenue for exploiting upcoming wide-field imaging surveys to systematically investigate dark matter substructures across large cluster samples, complementing traditional gravitational lensing techniques. Moreover, the model is inherently flexible and can incorporate multi-wavelength observations, including X-ray and Sunyaev--Zel'dovich data, to further improve total mass predictions.

papers.title: Probing baryonic feedback using fast radio bursts and galaxy surveys
papers.authors: Haruki Ebina, Martin White
papers.abstract: The dispersion measure (DM) of fast radio bursts (FRB) provides a noisy measure of the free-electron column density to the burst. With next-generation FRB surveys the number of bursts will drastically increase and measurements of the baryon distribution will be possible on the Mpc scales most relevant to Stage IV weak lensing surveys. Comparing the DM auto-spectrum, DM-shear cross-spectrum and the kinetic Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect, we argue that the cross-correlation of FRB catalogs with galaxy surveys offers many advantages. Hybrid Effective Field Theory (HEFT), often used in large-scale structure cosmology, is capable of modeling the clustering of electrons jointly with galaxies and matter to small scales. Using HEFT with the Padé model of baryonic feedback, we forecast that next-generation FRB surveys (combined with galaxy samples) will be able to constrain feedback at a level informative for Stage IV weak lensing surveys. In particular we should not be limited by modeling the manner in which galaxies trace the matter field. Rather constraints of the higher-order electron biases and the electron-galaxy cross-stochasticity provide the dominant limitation, and are an obvious target for improvement in order to reach percent-level constraints. The same measurements also provide a valuable means of constraining feedback in hydrodynamic simulations of galaxy formation in a way that is not tied to the modeling of particular galaxy samples.

Within the HEFT framework, galaxy bias uncertainties do not limit baryonic feedback constraints because the 3D galaxy clustering ($P_\ell^{gg}$) is sample-variance limited and self-calibrates the galaxy-matter connection on the relevant scales ($0.1 < k < 1\,h\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}$).

papers.title: Parity conservation of the isotropic galaxy 4PCF in redshift space
papers.authors: Chanasorn Kongprachaya, Nicola Bartolo, Daniele Bertacca, Sabino Matarrese
papers.abstract: Recent observational investigation of cosmological Parity Violation (PV) through the galaxy Four-point Correlation Function (4PCF) has motivated a careful theoretical examination of potential systematic contributions. In this work, we demonstrate that parity-odd contributions to the isotropic 4PCF estimator induced by Redshift Space Distortion (RSD), up to the leading order $\mathcal{H}/k$ of general relativistic corrections, vanish upon averaging over all the Line-of-Sight (LOS). We analyse the perturbative relativistic galaxy number density, combining the biased tracer expansion and the dark matter gravitational dynamics within the framework of Standard Eulerian Perturbation Theory (EPT) to third order in the density perturbation. Building on prior studies of the parity-odd mode of the trispectrum (the Fourier-space counterpart of the 4PCF), we extend existing results in three directions: incorporating the wide-angle effect by adopting a local LOS definition for each galaxy in the 4PCF, accounting for tidal bias in the galaxy population, and generalising the assessment to an arbitrary cosmological background. Expanding the 4PCF in spherical harmonics, we show that angular momentum selection rules, encoded in the Wigner 3-j symbols, enforce that only parity-even contributions survive the integration over all LOS orientations, both in the plane-parallel approximation and in the full wide-angle case. This result is crucial for large-scale statistical analyses using isotropic estimators. It supports interpreting possible PV detections as a signal not due to a systematic RSD artefact. We conclude with a discussion of the caveats of our results and identify potential sources of PV.

By expanding the 4PCF into spherical harmonics, the authors prove that angular momentum selection rules (via Wigner 3-$j$ symbols) strictly eliminate all parity-odd terms both in the standard plane-parallel approximation and when incorporating wide-angle effects (assigning each galaxy in the quartet its own local LOS).

This exact cancellation holds even when extending the third-order Eulerian Perturbation Theory (EPT) framework to include tidal galaxy bias and an arbitrary cosmological expansion history (where the growth rate $f$ is a free function rather than restricted to Einstein-de Sitter).

Consequently, recent observational hints of parity violation in BOSS ($2.9\sigma\text{--}7\sigma$) and DESI ($4\sigma\text{--}10\sigma$) cannot be explained away as an intrinsic RSD or wide-angle projection artefact, though partial sky coverage (survey masks), unequal-time effects ($\Delta z \lesssim 0.05$), or higher-order GR effects like lensing could still leak residual parity-odd signals.

papers.title: Does Dark Energy Evolve $\textit{and}$ Cluster?
papers.authors: Maria Luisa Gallavotti, Alessandra Silvestri
papers.abstract: Recent cosmological observations have renewed interest in dynamical dark energy, and naturally raise the question of whether departures from the standard expansion history are accompanied by modifications of gravitational dynamics. We address this question through a joint, non-parametric reconstruction of the effective dark-energy contribution to the expansion and the gravitational responses governing clustering and lensing, complemented by a combined covariance-mode analysis, without imposing model-specific relations between the sectors. Combining CMB, DESI DR2 BAO, and Pantheon+ supernova observations, and subsequently adding large scale structure observations including DES Year 3 $6\times2$pt data and other surveys, we recover a broad maximum in the effective dark-energy density near $z\simeq0.6$--$0.7$. The gravitational responses exhibit suggestive low-redshift enhancements over their GR values, approximately coincident with the background feature. Adding large scale structure information preserves the background feature but favours a mildly reduced lensing response. The combined covariance-mode analysis identifies the combinations of background and gravitational responses most tightly constrained by current observations and quantifies their departures from $\Lambda$CDM. The leading modes are decisively background dominated, while the gravitational sector remains less precisely constrained. Thus, present data cannot yet determine whether the suggestive low-redshift features in the two sectors share a common physical origin, a question that ongoing Stage-IV surveys will be able to address

In the baseline analysis (CMB + DESI BAO + Pantheon+), both the clustering response $\mu$ and lensing response $\Sigma$ show suggestive $\sim 20\%$ enhancements above the GR value of $1$ at low redshifts ($z \lesssim 1$), roughly coinciding with the peak in $\Omega_{\rm X}(z)$.

Adding LSS data (DES Y3 $6\times2$pt and SDSS RSD) preserves the mild enhancement in $\mu > 1$ but shifts the lensing parameter $\Sigma < 1$, indicating weaker gravitational lensing per unit matter fluctuation without shifting the inferred $S_8$ parameter.

In the combined covariant principal-component analysis (CPCA), the strongest departures from $\Lambda\text{CDM}$ occur in background-dominated modes with signal-to-noise ratio $\text{SNR} \simeq 2.3$, whereas lensing-dominated ($\Sigma$) modes show only weak departures ($\text{SNR} \simeq 1.3$). Current data precision is therefore insufficient to confirm whether the background and perturbation features share a common modified-gravity origin.

papers.title: Depletion of Dark Matter Spikes by Massive Black Hole Mergers
papers.authors: Charlie Sharpe, Thomas F. M. Spieksma, Yonadav Barry Ginat, Ricarda S. Beckmann, Alexander Heger, Bence Kocsis
papers.abstract: Dark matter over-densities around massive black holes, known as dark matter spikes, can dephase gravitational waves emitted by intermediate- and extreme-mass-ratio inspirals (IMRIs/EMRIs), offering a promising way to indirectly detect dark matter. This detection channel, however, requires the spike to survive over cosmological time-scales. We investigate the impact that a host black hole's merger history has on its dark-matter spike. We focus on how the inspiral of a massive-black-hole (MBH) binary modifies and disrupts these spikes within the central $\sim 100$ Schwarzschild radii of the black hole. We find that a single merger with mass ratio $q = 0.03$ is capable of reducing a spike's density by around 3 (5) orders of magnitude at 100 (5) Schwarzschild radii across all polar angles relative to the binary's plane, independent of the primary MBH's mass, with larger mass ratios inducing even stronger depletion. In fact, a single past merger with mass ratio as small as $q = 0.005$ reduces central densities by 2--3 orders of magnitude, making gravitational-wave dephasing difficult to detect. We relate these results to the MBH merger history by analysing cosmological simulation data from Horizon-AGN. We find that mergers become increasingly common as the MBH mass increases, with mergers of mass ratio q > 0.03 having occurred in 50% of MBHs of mass $3\times10^7M_\odot$ and 95% of mass $10^8M_\odot$ at z=0. These fractions are reached at even lighter masses ($2\times10^7M_\odot$ and $5\times10^7M_\odot$, respectively) at z=3. We find that accretion-induced adiabatic MBH growth is unable to cause appreciable spike re-growth between such mergers in {\tt Horizon-AGN}. Thus, in combination with previous studies of EMRI-induced depletion, this work constrains the mass range over which massive black holes can host detectable DM spikes to $10^6M_\odot$--$5 \times 10^7M_\odot$ for $z \leq 3$.

Even mergers as small as $q = 0.005$ reduce central densities by 2–3 orders of magnitude.

In the Horizon-AGN cosmological simulation, the fraction of MBHs that have undergone at least one $q \geq 0.03$ merger increases with mass: at $z=0$, $\sim 50\%$ of MBHs with $M_{\rm BH} = 3\times 10^7\,M_\odot$ and $\sim 95\%$ with $M_{\rm BH} = 10^8\,M_\odot$ have experienced a spike-destroying merger (shifting to $2\times 10^7\,M_\odot$ and $5\times 10^7\,M_\odot$ at $z=3$).

papers.title: Simple multi-interacting fluids in SymBoltz
papers.authors: David Figueruelo, Herman Sletmoen
papers.abstract: We implement a simple and general way of specifying arbitrary interactions between baryons, dark matter and dark energy in the Einstein--Boltzmann code SymBoltz. Due to the symbolic-numeric interface and approximation-free structure of SymBoltz, the model definition is remarkably compact and convenient to modify by specifying only the covariant coupling. The full equations are stiff, but stable and fast to integrate with an efficient implicit solver, particularly with the sparse and analytical ODE Jacobian generated from the symbolic equations. We first validate it using single-interaction models, comparing their background evolution and matter and CMB power spectra with those from modified versions of CLASS, finding $0.1\%$--$1\%$ agreement at most scales. Finally, we show how our framework makes it trivial to implement models with any interactions of any complexity among all three species simultaneously, which requires a more involved implementation in other Einstein--Boltzmann codes like CLASS or CAMB. Our full model is specified in only around 300 lines of code and is easy to modify for any other interaction by just specifying it in three lines.

The authors account for local expansion perturbations by replacing the unperturbed Hubble rate $H$ with the covariant expansion scalar $\Theta = \nabla_\mu u^\mu$ evaluated in the total energy frame, ensuring full relativistic consistency at linear order.

Validation of single-interaction models against modified versions of CLASS demonstrates $0.1\%$–$1\%$ agreement across most scales for the background evolution, linear matter power spectrum, and CMB angular power spectra, while easily extending to simultaneous three-species interactions.

They formulate a fully covariant interaction framework—properly perturbing the local expansion rate via the expansion scalar $\Theta = \nabla_\mu u^\mu$ in the total energy frame—where users only need to specify three symbolic quantities per interaction pair: the background energy transfer $\bar{Q}$, its perturbation $\delta Q$, and the momentum transfer potential $f$. This allows arbitrary, simultaneous interactions among baryons, dark matter, and dark energy to be added in just three lines of code, providing a rapid, bug-resistant way to generate linear power spectra for complex interacting dark sector models.

papers.title: Mapping the Evolving Cosmic Web on the Lightcone with WebON: HOLI Mock Strategy
papers.authors: Francisco-Shu Kitaura, Francesco Sinigaglia, Kilian Peraza Vera, Pere Rosselló, Daniel Forero-Sánchez, Natalia Villa-Nova Rodrigues, Jorge E. García-Farieta, Yunyi Tang, Jose María Coloma-Nadal, Ginevra Favole, Aurelio Carnero-Rosell, Cheng Zhao, Kentaro Nagamine
papers.abstract: Wide-area spectroscopic surveys such as DESI require large ensembles of mock catalogues that follow gravitational evolution and tracer populations across the observer's past lightcone. We present WebON (Web ON the lightcone), a fast method for mapping the evolving dark-matter cosmic web onto the lightcone without periodic-box replication or the stitching of separately evolved snapshot shells. Displacements computed at a limited set of redshifts are combined with a particle-wise Zel'dovich estimate of the emission redshift and a continuous-redshift correction, allowing lightcone positions to be generated in a single forward pass. The method supports regularised ALPT and eALPT gravity solvers, with an optional short-range ridging correction. We illustrate full-sky matter and cosmic-web evolution and find percent-level agreement between lightcone and fixed-redshift angular power spectra over the tested redshift and multipole ranges, providing an internal consistency check of the lightcone construction. Optional modules address approximate relativistic position corrections and local primordial non-Gaussianity. Finally, we show how the spectral cosmic-web hierarchy connects WebON to the HOLI (Higher Order LIghtcone) mock strategy, in which post-processing ridging and calibrated HICOBIAN bias and subgrid prescriptions can recover tracer clustering beyond the nominal resolution of the ALPT matter field. Independent comparisons of ridged LPT matter fields with Abacus N -body simulations and published percent-level tests of the hierarchical tracer-bias model complement the lightcone consistency measurements presented here.

conclusions: WebON constructs seamless observer-centred dark-matter lightcones in a single forward pass by estimating particle emission redshifts via Zel'dovich displacements and applying a linear LPT increment to nearby stored snapshots, avoiding shell-stitching discontinuities and box replication.

Internal consistency checks show percent-level agreement between the continuous lightcone angular power spectra $C_\ell$ and fixed-redshift snapshot references across the tested redshift shells and multipole ranges.

By combining the evolved matter fields with a spectral hierarchy of cosmic-web operators (using tidal $k^{-2}$ and density-curvature $k^0$ Hessians to define 16 environmental subregions) and the HICOBIAN field-level bias model, the HOLI pipeline recovers halo power spectra to better than $2\%$ accuracy up to $k \simeq 0.8\,h\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}$ from coarse ($1\text{--}6\,h^{-1}\,\mathrm{Mpc}$) ALPT meshes.

Optional ultra-large-scale modules incorporate an approximate relativistic position-level gauge transformation ($\mathbf{\Psi}_{\rm GR} \propto \ell^{-2}(z)\nabla\nabla^{-4}\delta$) and local primordial non-Gaussianity ($f_{\rm NL}^{\rm loc}$), where an 8-weight environmental cosmic-web reweighting scheme successfully emulates the characteristic $k^{-2}$ scale-dependent bias response across $f_{\rm NL}^{\rm loc} \in [-100, 100]$.
