ai.summary: Wide-area spectroscopic surveys like DESI and Euclid require thousands of mock galaxy catalogues across the observer's past lightcone—where lookback time and gravitational evolution vary continuously with distance—to estimate covariance matrices and test systematics, a task far too computationally expensive for full $N$-body simulations. To bypass this bottleneck, the authors present WebON (Web ON the lightcone), a fast approximate gravity framework based on Augmented Lagrangian Perturbation Theory (ALPT, which combines second-order LPT with spherical-collapse small-scale regularisation) that maps dark matter particles directly onto a continuous lightcone without replicating periodic boxes or stitching together discrete snapshot shells. WebON estimates each particle's lightcone-crossing redshift using a first-order Zel'dovich displacement proxy and interpolates between a sparse set of stored ALPT displacement snapshots via a linear growth correction, optionally sharpening dense filaments ("ridging") and adding ultra-large-scale general relativistic position shifts or local primordial non-Gaussianity ($f_{\rm NL}^{\rm loc}$). Finally, the authors demonstrate how WebON serves as the backbone for the HOLI (Higher Order LIghtcone) mock pipeline, which classifies the cosmic web across multiple spatial scales (combining long-range tidal and short-range density-curvature tensors) to apply a calibrated field-level bias model (HICOBIAN) that accurately populates coarse dark-matter fields with galaxies.

papers.title: Microscopic Realizability of Non-unique Bubble Hydrodynamics
papers.authors: Giulio Barni, Eric Madge
papers.abstract: First-order phase transitions drive fluid motion that induces energy transport and gravitational-wave production. The flows are usually classified in terms of the wall velocity and the transition strength. We show that this description fails when the two phases have unequal sound speeds $c_\pm$. New mixed-hybrid profiles may appear, and for a strong hierarchy, $c_+\gg c_-$, where the phase behind the wall is much softer, heating or cooling ahead of the wall allow for the coexistence of distinct stationary flows at the same wall velocity and transition strength. This ambiguity is removed once thermodynamic normalization and entropy production are specified. We identify microscopic settings that realize these sound-speed hierarchies. In thermal plasmas it requires exponentially large mass-to-temperature ratios, whereas at finite density a conserved charge removes this obstruction, making dense matter its natural arena.

conclusions: When the sound speed ahead of the bubble wall exceeds that behind it ($c_+ > c_-$), a new class of "mixed-hybrid" fluid profiles emerges where the flow reverses direction across the wall, and for strong hierarchies ($c_+ \gg c_-$), up to three distinct profiles can coexist at the same $(\xi_w, \alpha_N)$ (e.g., at benchmark $c_+ = 0.9, c_- = 0.16$).

This hydrodynamic degeneracy is an artifact of an incomplete macroscopic parametrization and is uniquely resolved once the relative effective thermal degrees of freedom ($\Psi_N \equiv w_-(T_N)/w_+(T_N)$) and the entropy production across the wall are specified.

In zero-density thermal plasmas, enthalpy flux conservation forces heavy particles behind the wall to heat up so strongly that $c_+/c_-$ grows only as $\sqrt{\ln(m/T_+)}$, requiring extreme mass-to-temperature ratios ($m/T_+ \simeq 70$ for fold onset and $\sim 10^9$ for $c_+/c_- \simeq 5$) that make strong hierarchies difficult to realize in early-Universe radiation plasmas or $SU(3)$ confining transitions.

At finite chemical potential, a conserved charge decouples enthalpy transport from thermal heating, allowing realistic sound-speed hierarchies in cold, dense environments—such as a transition from stiff hadronic matter ($c_+ \simeq 0.75$) to softer quark matter ($c_- \lesssim 0.35$) inside neutron-star cores.
ai.summary: Cosmological first-order phase transitions proceed via the nucleation and expansion of bubbles of a new vacuum phase, driving relativistic fluid shocks and rarefaction waves that source a stochastic gravitational-wave background. Standard hydrodynamic models assume a radiation-like "bag" equation of state where both phases share the conformal sound speed $c_s = 1/\sqrt{3}$, which guarantees that a bubble's fluid profile is uniquely determined by just the bubble wall velocity $\xi_w$ and the transition strength $\alpha_N$. In this paper, the authors generalize the relativistic hydrodynamic matching conditions to phases with unequal constant sound speeds ($c_+$ ahead of the wall and $c_-$ behind it) and investigate what microscopic particle physics systems can actually produce strong sound-speed hierarchies. They show that when the phase behind the wall is much softer ($c_+ \gg c_-$), heating or cooling upstream of the wall can compensate for different local wall states, causing up to three distinct fluid profiles (including flows moving in opposite directions) to coexist at the exact same $(\xi_w, \alpha_N)$ until the relative thermal degrees of freedom and entropy production at the wall are specified. Exploring microscopic realizations, they find that early-Universe thermal plasmas at zero chemical potential struggle to reach this regime, whereas cold, dense matter with a conserved charge (such as hadron-to-quark phase transitions in neutron stars) realizes it naturally.

papers.title: HydróDex: gotta match 'em all!
papers.authors: Giulio Barni, Eric Madge
papers.abstract: We present a comprehensive hydrodynamic classification of stationary fluid profiles in first-order phase transitions within the constant-sound-speed model, a physically motivated extension of the standard bag model that allows the sound speeds in front of and behind the wall, $c_+$ and $c_-$, to differ. Solving the matching conditions at the bubble wall and evolving the profile in the surrounding plasma, we systematically identify and classify all the possible stationary solutions. The classification recovers all previously known direct and inverse detonation, deflagration, and hybrid solutions, while revealing a new class of stationary configurations, termed mixed hybrids, featuring rarefaction waves on both sides of the wall and oppositely directed fluid flows. For a sufficiently pronounced hierarchy $c_+ > c_-$, the classification in terms of the wall velocity $\xi_w$ and the asymptotic strength parameter $\alpha_N$ further exhibits degenerate regions in parameter space, where multiple distinct stationary profiles correspond to the same physical inputs $(\xi_w,\alpha_N)$. This non-uniqueness arises as the parametrization discards thermodynamic information and is resolved once the underlying microphysics is specified. We also compute the kinetic-energy budget and the associated acoustic gravitational-wave spectra within the sound-shell model, finding that mixed-hybrid solutions, despite their oppositely directed flows, introduce no additional spectral feature, and their spectra can be closely mimicked by ordinary direct or inverse hybrids with very different fluid profiles. Finally, we release HydróDex, a public code that implements the complete hydrodynamic classification, fluid-profile construction, kinetic-energy budget, and gravitational-wave calculation.

conclusions: Allowing unequal sound speeds ($c_+ \neq c_-$) reveals a new "mixed hybrid" hydrodynamic branch when the wall speed lies between the two sound speeds ($c_- < \xi_w < c_+$), featuring rarefaction waves on both sides of the bubble wall and fluid velocities that reverse direction across the interface.

For a sufficiently large sound-speed hierarchy ($c_+ / c_- \gg 1$), the mapping from the local transition strength at the wall ($\alpha_+$) to the asymptotic strength in the unperturbed plasma ($\alpha_N$) becomes non-monotonic, creating degenerate parameter regions where up to three distinct stationary fluid profiles coexist for the same $(\xi_w, \alpha_N)$ inputs.

This apparent non-uniqueness is an artifact of the reduced hydrodynamic parameterization discarding thermodynamic normalization and wall entropy production; specifying the full microscopic equation of state in local thermal equilibrium lifts the degeneracy and selects a single physical branch.

Within the sound-shell model, mixed-hybrid fluid profiles produce a single-peaked acoustic gravitational-wave spectrum without unique spectral signatures, meaning their GW signals can be closely mimicked by ordinary direct or inverse hybrids even with opposite signs of $\alpha_N$.
ai.summary: During a cosmological first-order phase transition in the early Universe, bubbles of a new vacuum phase nucleate and expand through the primordial plasma, stirring up relativistic fluid flows and sound waves that source a stochastic gravitational-wave background. Standard hydrodynamical models use the "bag equation of state," which assumes both the old and new phases are radiation-like fluids with identical sound speeds ($c_s = 1/\sqrt{3}$), whereas realistic particle physics models often feature different sound speeds ahead of ($c_+$) and behind ($c_-$) the bubble wall. In this paper, the authors use the constant-speed-of-sound (CSS) model ($c_+ \neq c_-$) to systematically classify all stationary, self-similar relativistic fluid profiles around expanding spherical bubbles and release a fast C++/Python code, `HydróDex`, to compute these profiles and their resulting gravitational-wave spectra. By relaxing the equal-sound-speed assumption, they discover a new family of "mixed hybrid" fluid flows and show how mapping local wall conditions to macroscopic transition parameters can become non-unique when $c_+ \gg c_-$.

papers.title: Many-body Response to Spin-Independent and Spin-Dependent Dark Matter Scattering in a Superfluid Helium-3 Target
papers.authors: A. Ting, N. Darvishi, S. Autti, L. Bloomfield, A. Casey, N. Eng, P. Franchini, R. P. Haley, P. J. Heikkinen, A. Jennings, A. Kemp, E. Leason, J. March-Russell, J. Monroe, D. Münstermann, M.T. Noble, J. R. Prance, X. Rojas, T. Salmon, J. Saunders, J. Smirnov, R. Smith, M. D. Thompson, A. Thomson, V. Tsepelin, S. M. West, L. Whitehead, D. E. Zmeev
papers.abstract: The QUEST-DMC experiment employs an ultra-low-temperature superfluid $^3$He target in an effort to detect sub-GeV dark matter (DM). The low-momentum scattering of such light DM is sensitive to the many-body structure of superfluid $^3$He, making it necessary to account for the collective behaviour of the medium. We present a first-principles calculation of the DM scattering rate in this inherently quantum many-body medium for both spin-independent and spin-dependent interactions. The leading consequence of this many-body behaviour is a kinematic enhancement of the scattering rate arising from the Fermi-Dirac statistics of the ultra-low-temperature target. Accounting for this extends the projected reach to lower DM masses for both spin-independent and spin-dependent interactions under the benchmark detector assumptions considered here. The resulting sensitivity improvement becomes increasingly pronounced as the detector threshold drops into the sub-eV regime. It is negligible at the conventional readout threshold of approximately $31$ eV, but becomes significant at the $0.51$ eV benchmark threshold for SQUID-based readout. Specifically, at this threshold, incorporating the many-body response extends the higher-energy recoil tail and improves the projected low-mass reach by approximately $2.5\%$ relative to the single-atom approximation. This improvement becomes more pronounced at lower thresholds. Reaching a threshold of $5$ meV could further extend the sensitivity of QUEST-DMC into the realm of sub-MeV DM.

conclusions: For momentum transfers comparable to the Fermi momentum of the $^3\text{He}$ target, the finite initial momenta of the fermions produce a higher-energy recoil tail that allows lighter dark matter particles to exceed the detector threshold than predicted by the single-atom approximation.

At the benchmark SQUID-based readout threshold of $0.51\text{ eV}$, accounting for the many-body quantum response improves the projected low-mass reach of QUEST-DMC by approximately $2.5\%$ (around $m_\chi \lesssim 10\text{ MeV}/c^2$), whereas at the conventional $31\text{ eV}$ readout threshold the effect is negligible.

Pushing detector thresholds down to $5\text{ meV}$ could extend QUEST-DMC's sensitivity into the sub-MeV dark matter regime, though at very low momentum transfers ($q \ll k_F$) Pauli blocking suppresses the available phase space and effectively reduces the fiducial target mass.

At high momentum transfers ($q \gg k_F$, corresponding to $m_\chi \gtrsim 20\text{ MeV}/c^2$ and recoil energies above $1\text{ eV}$), the many-body dynamic structure functions for both spin-independent and spin-dependent interactions smoothly recover the standard incoherent single-atom scattering rate, validating previous sensitivity projections.
ai.summary: Direct detection experiments searching for light, sub-GeV dark matter (DM) require ultra-low energy thresholds because light DM particles transfer very little momentum when scattering off atomic nuclei. The QUEST-DMC experiment uses a superfluid Helium-3 ($^3\text{He}$) target cooled below $200\ \mu\text{K}$, where the de Broglie wavelength of MeV-scale DM becomes comparable to the nanometre-scale interatomic spacing and Fermi wavelength of the medium, meaning the DM interacts with a coherent quantum many-body system rather than isolated atoms at rest. In this paper, the authors perform a first-principles calculation of both spin-independent and spin-dependent DM scattering rates in the superfluid $^3\text{He}$ B-phase by deriving the medium's dynamic structure functions via Bogoliubov quasiparticle excitations of the Cooper-pair condensate. Because $^3\text{He}$ atoms are fermions, quantum degeneracy pressure (Fermi-Dirac statistics) forces the target atoms to have finite initial momenta even in the ground state, which kinematically boosts the maximum recoil energy a light DM particle can deposit and extends the experiment's sensitivity to lower DM masses.

papers.title: Probing the Activity History of Repeating Fast Radio Bursts with Cluster Lensing
papers.authors: Huan Zhou, Kai Liao, Zhengxiang Li, Cheng-Gang Shao
papers.abstract: Fast radio bursts (FRBs) are millisecond duration coherent radio transients, some of whose sources repeat, but the nature and active lifetimes of their engines remain uncertain. Strong lensing by galaxy clusters provides a physical lever on this lifetime problem: a short campaign can sample emission epochs of a repeating FRB separated by years, and distinct bursts in different lensed images, given a known relative lens delay, set a lower bound on its active lifetime, whereas delayed copies of a single burst only encode the lens delay. Based on the cluster-lens model of MACS J0717.5+3745, we quantify the accessible range of emission epochs for finite activity episodes, observing windows, and discovery selection. For a source-frame episode of duration \(100~{\rm yr}\) at \(z_s=2\) and a source-frame rate of \(0.1\,{\rm h}_{\rm src}^{-1}\), a five year campaign conditional on discovery yields a \(95\%\) gain threshold of \(m_{95}\simeq25.6\), corresponding to a source-frame span of \(L_{95}\simeq42.6~{\rm yr}\). At the population level, combining distinct burst associations with same burst echoes provides a way to test specified activity durations with a finite lens catalogue, e.g., activity durations differing by an order of magnitude can be distinguished with expected Bayes factor above $20$. More broadly, these lensed source frame epochs enable applications beyond activity-duration tests, e.g., linking burst activity to the evolution of the engine and its environment. Galaxy-cluster lensing therefore provides a promising future probe for accessing otherwise unobserved source history and for distinguishing between different activity duration models.

conclusions: For a repeating FRB at $z_s=2$ with a $100\text{ yr}$ active phase and a burst rate of $0.1\text{ h}_{\text{src}}^{-1}$, a 5-year monitoring campaign of MACS J0717.5+3745 can probe up to $L_{95} \simeq 42.6\text{ yr}$ of source-frame history (a $95\%$ gain threshold of $m_{95} \simeq 25.6$ over the single-image baseline), with a theoretical geometric ceiling of $79.3\text{ yr}$ for this cluster.

Using all lensed images instead of just a single reference image boosts the expected number of detected distinct intrinsic bursts by up to a factor of $R_N \approx 2\text{--}3$ for long-lived, high-rate sources.

A joint Bayesian analysis of only $N=10$ strongly lensed repeating FRBs—combining distinct-burst pairs and same-burst echoes—can distinguish between engine activity durations that differ by an order of magnitude with strong evidence ($\mathbb{E}[\ln B_{12}] > 3$, or Bayes factor $> 20$).

Comparing distinct bursts and echoes across multiple lensed images allows observers to separate intrinsic decades-long secular evolution in the source's local plasma environment (via dispersion and rotation measures) or persistent radio nebula from static line-of-sight propagation differences.
ai.summary: Fast radio bursts (FRBs) are brief, intense flashes of radio emission from distant galaxies; while some FRB sources repeat, we do not know whether their central engines (such as magnetars or accreting compact objects) stay active for years, decades, or centuries because telescope monitoring campaigns only last a few years. This paper proposes using strong gravitational lensing by galaxy clusters—where light from a single background source takes multiple paths with relative time delays of decades—as a natural "time machine" to sample an FRB's activity across much longer source-frame baselines during a short observing campaign. Using mass reconstructions of the Hubble Frontier Fields cluster MACS J0717.5+3745 and realistic daily-transit observing windows, the authors model two types of lensed detections: "Class II" echoes (the exact same burst arriving in different images) and "Class I" pairs (two distinct bursts from the same source seen in different images, which directly bound the active lifetime once the lens time delay is subtracted). This framework shows that cluster lensing can extend the accessible history of repeating FRBs from a few years to several decades, allowing astronomers to distinguish between competing progenitor engine models and track long-term evolution in the burst's local plasma environment.

papers.title: bihalofit-JAX: A Differentiable Code for the Nonlinear Matter Bispectrum and its Projected Statistics
papers.authors: Alexander Roskill, Matteo Zennaro
papers.abstract: Theoretical predictions for the nonlinear matter bispectrum and related projected statistics have been historically very expensive to evaluate, leading many analyses to rely on emulators to speed up slow numerical codes. We show in this paper that this need not be the case: improved numerical techniques can be leveraged to directly evaluate predictions for the nonlinear matter bispectrum and projected statistics at speeds preferable for inference. We present bihalofit-JAX, an open-source, fully differentiable code for the nonlinear matter bispectrum based on the BiHalofit fitting formula, which includes numerous related projected statistics such as angular bispectra, skew spectra and aperture statistics. It computes $10000$ triangles of the matter bispectrum in $\sim1$--$2\ \rm{ms}$ per cosmology, one to three orders of magnitude faster than other implementations. It agrees numerically with the original BiHalofit code to better than $0.02\%$ on average over the cosmologies the formula was calibrated on, where the formula itself is accurate to $\sim20\%$ against simulations. It is also efficiently vectorised such that one can compute e.g. $500$ cosmologies in $\sim 2\ \rm{ms}$. This speed-up grows even more in the case of the third-order aperture statistics, which we compute in $\sim 6\ \rm{ms}$ for one cosmology, between $3\times10^3$ and $2.4\times10^4$ times faster than other publicly available codes. The pipeline is fully differentiable, and we demonstrate its performance in a simple inference problem, comparing the No-U-Turn Sampler (NUTS) to gradient-free inference with the affine-invariant ensemble sampler (emcee).

conclusions: The code computes $10{,}000$ triangles of the 3D matter bispectrum in $\sim 1\text{--}2\ \mathrm{ms}$ per cosmology and batches $500$ cosmologies in $\sim 2\ \mathrm{ms}$ (up to $4\times 10^3$ times faster than the next fastest implementation), while agreeing with the original BiHalofit code to better than $0.02\%$ on average (well within the $\sim 20\%$ simulation-calibration accuracy of the formula itself).

For projected third-order aperture-mass statistics ($\langle M_{\mathrm{ap}}^3 \rangle$), which require costly nested integrals over the bispectrum, `bihalofit-JAX` achieves an evaluation time of $\sim 6\ \mathrm{ms}$ per cosmology—a speedup of $3\times 10^3$ to $2.4\times 10^4$ times over existing public codes.

The package integrates three interchangeable, differentiable linear power spectrum backends (`baccoemu`, the symbolic-regression formula `syren-new`, and Eisenstein & Hu), finding that `baccoemu` and `syren-new` agree on the resulting matter bispectrum to $0.2\%$ on average, though `syren-new` is recommended for gradient-based sampling because its analytic form avoids the discontinuous derivatives caused by ReLU activations in `baccoemu`.

Because the entire pipeline is end-to-end differentiable and avoids the training overhead and parameter-space boundaries of neural-network emulators, it enables direct gradient-based Bayesian inference (demonstrated using the No-U-Turn Sampler, NUTS, compared against gradient-free `emcee`).
ai.relevance_reason: This paper (co-authored by Matteo Zennaro) presents a fast, GPU-accelerated, differentiable pipeline for non-linear LSS summary statistics and critically examines when direct JAX-optimised numerical evaluation can replace or baseline cosmological emulators.
ai.summary: While the matter power spectrum measures two-point clustering, gravitational collapse generates non-Gaussian filamentary and halo structures whose information is captured by the bispectrum (the three-point correlation function in Fourier space). Evaluating the non-linear matter bispectrum—and especially its line-of-sight projections for weak lensing and galaxy clustering, such as angular bispectra, skew spectra, and third-order aperture-mass statistics—requires nested integrals that have historically been too slow for MCMC inference without training neural-network emulators. In this paper, the authors introduce `bihalofit-JAX`, an open-source, GPU-accelerated, and fully differentiable implementation of the BiHalofit fitting formula (an analytic halo-model and perturbation-theory fit calibrated to $N$-body simulations for $w_0 w_a\text{CDM}$ and baryonic feedback). By replacing adaptive integration and bisection root-finding with fixed-iteration safeguarded Newton solvers and fixed Gauss–Legendre quadrature grids in JAX, the entire pipeline compiles once, vectorises across cosmologies and triangles, and propagates exact gradients from projected observables back to cosmological parameters. This demonstrates that careful numerical design on modern hardware can completely bypass the need to build and train surrogate emulators for complex higher-order summary statistics.

papers.title: Gravitational production of dark QED by the trace anomaly
papers.authors: Simon Cléry, Aliaksei Kachanovich, Michel HG Tytgat
papers.abstract: We revisit the production of fermionic dark matter $\chi$ through the graviton portal, sourced by inflaton annihilation at the end of inflation. Because the production rate is helicity-suppressed, $\propto m_\chi^2$, the dark fermion must be very heavy to account for the observed relic abundance, $m_\chi \gtrsim 10^{10}$ GeV, with the exact bound set by the reheating temperature $T_{\rm RH}$. Here we examine how interactions within the dark sector could modify this result. As a toy model, we consider dark QED, in which $\chi$ couples to a light dark photon. We first show that, as a consequence of classical conformal invariance, bremsstrahlung of a dark photon does not lift the helicity suppression for light fermions. We then show that the trace anomaly of dark QED, which affects the coupling of the graviton to dark photons, can produce light dark fermions via a Dalitz process. This allows to extend the fermionic dark mass range possibly down to $m_\chi \sim 10^7$~GeV, depending on $T_{\rm RH}$ and the dark QED coupling. We also determine under which conditions the hidden sector reaches thermal equilibrium and derive a lower bound on the temperature ratio at reheating $(T'/T)_{\rm RH}$ as function of the dark QED coupling and the reheating temperature.

conclusions: Classical conformal invariance guarantees that tree-level dark photon bremsstrahlung ($\phi\phi \to \chi\bar{\chi}\gamma'$) has a traceless stress-energy tensor in the massless limit, meaning it cannot lift the $\propto m_\chi^2$ helicity suppression of gravitational fermion production.

At one-loop order, the dark QED trace anomaly induces an effective coupling between gravitons and massless dark photons, opening a 3-body Dalitz-like production channel ($\phi\phi \to \gamma' \chi\bar{\chi}$) that is logarithmically enhanced by $\log(m_\phi / m_\chi)$ when the fermion pair is collinear.

For an order-unity dark gauge coupling ($e' \simeq 1$) and high reheating temperatures ($T_{\rm RH} \sim 10^{14}\text{ GeV}$), this anomalous production channel lowers the dark matter mass required to match the observed relic density by 1–2 orders of magnitude, extending the viable range down to $m_\chi \sim 10^7\text{ GeV}$ (compared to $\gtrsim 10^{10}\text{ GeV}$ without dark sector interactions).

Giving the dark photon a small Stueckelberg mass ($10^{-20}\text{ eV} \lesssim m_{\gamma'} \lesssim 10^{-2}\text{ eV}$) evades long-range self-interaction bounds, while the gravitationally produced longitudinal modes decouple from the fermions and contribute negligibly to dark matter and dark radiation.
ai.summary: Even if dark matter resides in a completely hidden sector with no direct couplings to the Standard Model, it must still interact via gravity, allowing it to be produced at the end of inflation when oscillating inflaton particles annihilate through virtual gravitons (the "graviton portal"). For fermionic dark matter ($\chi$), this $s$-wave annihilation is normally "helicity-suppressed"—its rate scales with the fermion mass squared ($\propto m_\chi^2$) because the graviton couples to the trace of the stress-energy tensor, which vanishes for massless particles—forcing $\chi$ to be superheavy ($m_\chi \gtrsim 10^{10}\text{ GeV}$) to account for the observed relic abundance. The authors investigate whether adding dark sector interactions via a toy "dark QED" model (where $\chi$ couples to a light dark photon $\gamma'$) can bypass this suppression. They prove that simple tree-level radiative emission of a dark photon (bremsstrahlung) fails to lift the mass suppression due to classical conformal invariance, but show that a one-loop quantum effect—the trace anomaly—couples gravitons directly to dark photons and enables fermion production via an off-shell dark photon decay ($\phi\phi \to \gamma'\chi\bar{\chi}$, analogous to neutral pion Dalitz decay). This quantum anomaly channel opens up a new viable parameter space for lighter gravitationally produced dark matter and establishes lower bounds on the dark-to-visible temperature ratio $(T'/T)_{\rm RH}$ if the hidden sector thermalizes.

papers.title: Little Red Dots from Small-Scale Primordial Black Hole Clustering
papers.authors: Borui Zhang, Wei-Xiang Feng, Haipeng An
papers.abstract: The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) observations have identified a class of compact galaxies at high redshifts ($4 \lesssim z \lesssim 8$), dubbed "little red dots" (LRDs). The supermassive black holes (SMBHs) of $10^{5-8}{\rm\,M}_{\odot}$ in LRDs favor a heavy-seed origin. We propose a mechanism for their formation: Clusters of primordial black holes, formed through long-short mode coupling on small scales in the early Universe, undergo sequential mergers over extended timescales. This mechanism can evade cosmic microwave background distortions and result in heavy-seed SMBHs via runaway mergers. We employ Monte Carlo simulations to solve the Smoluchowski coagulation equation and determine the runaway merging timescale. The resulting stochastic gravitational wave background offers a distinctive signature of this process, and our model suggests highly spinning SMBHs at their formation if they inherit the spin residual of the cluster from tidal fields.

papers.title: Cosmological inference with halo clustering reconstructed from the redshift-space galaxy distribution
papers.authors: Ryuichiro Hada, Teppei Okumura
papers.abstract: Accurate modeling of small-scale redshift-space clustering is crucial for full-shape redshift-space distortion (RSD) analyses, where satellite galaxies contribute to one-halo terms and Finger-of-God distortions. We investigate halo reconstruction based on the cylinder grouping method of Okumura et al., Mon. Not. R. Astron. Soc. 469, 459 (2017), which selects an effective halo center tracer from the observed galaxy distribution, and how it impacts cosmological parameter inference. Using luminous red galaxy mock catalogs from the AbacusSummit simulations at $z=1.1$, we perform effective field theory (EFT)-based full-shape modeling of the power spectrum of the reconstructed-halo sample. We show that the dominant reconstruction-induced systematics can be described and incorporated within the standard EFT framework. In particular, a simple multipole-dependent rescaling inferred directly from the data on large scales captures the dominant effect, while residual small-scale changes are absorbed by the standard counterterm and stochastic sector, without introducing additional reconstruction-specific parameters. The reconstructed-halo sample yields unbiased constraints on cosmological parameters, including the growth rate $f\sigma_{s8}$ and Alcock-Paczynski parameters. Compared to the galaxy sample, it enables both improved robustness and increased statistical precision: at the fiducial limit of $k_{\max}=0.2\,h\,{\rm Mpc}^{-1}$, the uncertainty on $f\sigma_{s8}$ is reduced by more than $20\%$, while the high-$k_{\max}$ diagnostics show comparatively stable goodness of fit and nuisance parameters.

papers.title: Bispectrum BAO and the baryon-dark matter relative velocity
papers.authors: Adriana Nadal-Matosas, Héctor Gil-Marín, Licia Verde
papers.abstract: We evaluate the Baryon Acoustic Oscillation (BAO) signal in the bispectrum as a tool to detect and characterize the relative velocity effect. We extend the existing framework by presenting an updated model for the redshift-space tree-level bispectrum that comprehensively incorporates all relative velocity terms. We introduce a novel, unbiased technique to extract the isotropic BAO dilation parameter ($\alpha_{\rm iso}$) solely from the bispectrum monopole. Validated against N-body simulations, this template-based extraction successfully recovers the acoustic scale and enhances the statistical constraining power by $\sim30\%$, when analyzed in tandem with the pre-reconstruction power spectrum, offering a powerful complement to standard post-reconstruction pipelines. We quantify how individual relative velocity components distort both two- and three-point statistics. We find that these effects induce distinct systematic shifts in the extracted $\alpha_{\rm iso}$ between the two probes. We find systematic discrepancies of up to $2\%$ for $b_{v^2}=\pm0.05$ and up to $20\%$ for $b_{\delta^{bc}}\le-2$. This differences demonstrate that a direct comparison of independent power spectrum and bispectrum BAO measurements can break parameter degeneracies and isolate the amplitude of these biases. Finally, we provide a concrete prescription to detect and constrain the three associated relative velocity bias parameters, showing that a joint analysis is highly sensitive to the $b_{v^2}$ and $b_{\delta^{bc}}$ amplitudes. This establishes the bispectrum BAO as a robust cosmological probe for current and next-generation galaxy surveys, serving both as a cross-check for standard analyses and a crucial diagnostic tool against systematic biases.

papers.title: The road towards precision measurements of $H_0$ with bright sirens in the Einstein Telescope era
papers.authors: Chiara De Leo, Elsa M. Teixeira, Vivian Poulin
papers.abstract: Gravitational-wave standard sirens provide an independent probe of cosmic expansion since their luminosity distances are inferred directly from the gravitational-wave signal and, for bright sirens (BSs), the source redshifts are obtained through the identification of electromagnetic counterparts. In this work, we forecast the constraining power of future bright siren catalogues on the Hubble constant using simulated binary-neutron-star mergers detected by the Einstein Telescope with associated electromagnetic counterparts. We construct mock catalogues with different numbers of events and redshift distributions, with GW170817 as a reference BS, and analyse the resulting constraints within a flat $\Lambda$CDM cosmology. We find that, when bright sirens are used as a standalone probe, most of the information on $H_0$ is provided by low-redshift events, with the improvement in precision saturating for sources above $z \sim 1$; beyond that redshift, the constraining power of BSs is increasingly limited by the degeneracy with $\Omega_m$, which prevents further gains in precision on $H_0$. In this case, approximately $90$ low-redshift BSs are required to reach $\sigma_{H_0} \sim 1\,{\rm km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$, while about $45$ are sufficient for $\sigma_{H_0} \sim 2\,{\rm km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$. When external BAO information is included to reduce the $H_0 - \Omega_m$ degeneracy, intermediate-redshift sirens become more informative and the required number of events decreases substantially, to roughly $20$ and $15$ BSs for $\sigma_{H_0} \sim 1\,{\rm km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$ and $\sigma_{H_0} \sim 2\,{\rm km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$, respectively. These results highlight the importance of both electromagnetic counterpart identification and complementary background probes in making BSs a competitive, distance-ladder-independent test of the Hubble tension.

papers.title: Domain walls through different cosmologies
papers.authors: I. Dankovsky, D. Gorbunov, S. Ramazanov, A. Vikman
papers.abstract: We study properties of domain walls (DWs) arising in the model with a double well potential assuming different early universe cosmologies: from dust through stiff matter domination to the limit of effective Minkowski space. Using lattice simulations we demonstrate that evolution of DW networks exhibits an approximate universality with respect to the cosmological equation of state (EoS). Namely, the wall area inside a given large volume is mainly determined by the particle horizon, while details of cosmic expansion play a subdominant role. As it follows, particle horizon rather than the inverse Hubble rate is pivotal in DW evolution defining the network correlation length and hence its phenomenology, e.g., the characteristic wavelength of emitted gravitational waves (GWs). Formation of closed DWs is shown to be very sensitive to the cosmological EoS and hence violate the universality, but their contribution to the total network is too small to change the overall picture. The universality breaking is also observed in the spectral properties of GWs from annihilating (biased) DWs: i) the IR slope of the spectrum depends on the EoS parameter; ii) there is a plateau in the UV part of the spectrum, which gets more pronounced as one stiffens the EoS. However, the dependence on the EoS is rather weak in the near peak region, which is most relevant from the viewpoint of pulsar timing arrays and other searches for the stochastic GW background. For a selection of primordial cosmologies, we provide fitting formulae for the spectra near the peak.

papers.title: Dark Matter Constraints from Small-Scale Cosmic Structure
papers.authors: Ethan O. Nadler, Keir K. Rogers, Alex Drlica-Wagner
papers.abstract: Small-scale cosmic structure provides a powerful test of the fundamental nature of dark matter. A wide range of dark matter models impact matter clustering on small scales, including warm, fuzzy, and (self-)interacting dark matter. In these scenarios, dark matter physics such as free-streaming, wave interference, and self/Standard Model interactions alter the abundance and internal structure of dark matter halos. Cosmological and astrophysical probes of small-scale structure---including dwarf galaxies, strong lensing, the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest, stellar streams, and high-redshift galaxies---are therefore sensitive to these effects. Here, we review dark matter constraints provided by small-scale structure, focusing on observables that probe scales smaller than $\sim 1~\mathrm{Mpc}$, which define the frontier of current measurements. We summarize how these constraints have been translated to limits on microphysical dark matter models, and we discuss key modeling uncertainties and observational systematics. Finally, we highlight the growing importance of probe combination and simulation-based inference for this field, and we overview upcoming observational facilities that will sharpen small-scale structure tests of dark matter physics.

papers.title: Model-Independent Assessments of Tidal Alignment and Density-Weighting Dependence in Galaxy Intrinsic Alignments
papers.authors: Paul Rogozenski, Sukhdeep Singh, Jonathan Blazek, Rachel Mandelbaum, Hung-Jin Huang, Ananth Tenneti
papers.abstract: Intrinsic alignments (IA) of galaxies are an important source of systematic uncertainty in weak gravitational lensing measurements and also serve as a test for models of galaxy formation and evolution. These galaxy alignments are usually modeled assuming that the IA are sourced by the tidal fields around the galaxies. However, galaxy properties, like their proximity to other galaxies and their mass, provide alignment contributions beyond the tidal field. In this work, we perform novel model-agnostic tests to determine the impact of density-weighting on the IA of galaxies using data from the IllustrisTNG cosmological hydrodynamical simulation and SDSS-III (BOSS). We show that the primary effect of density-weighting is an increase of the alignment amplitude at large scales, whereas the small-scale impact is sample-dependent. We also assess the tidal alignment paradigm for IllustrisTNG galaxies using two-point correlation functions of galaxy shapes, tidal fields, and the sampled background tidal field of the simulation box. We find, given the precision of our measurements, that central galaxies align linearly to the underlying (non-linear) tidal field well into the 1-halo regime.

papers.title: Minimal vacuum histories beyond $Λ$CDM: model comparison within VCDM
papers.authors: Antonio De Felice, Eleonora Di Valentino, Luis A. Escamilla, Jack Zidich
papers.abstract: Recent cosmological observations motivate alternatives to $\Lambda$CDM with evolving dark energy. We compare three such models, each introducing one additional cosmological parameter: F42, with equation of state $w(a)=w_0/\sqrt{a}$, and two smooth sign-changing effective dark-energy profiles, Ag and Qui. All models are implemented within VCDM, which determines the background and linear perturbations without introducing an additional propagating gravitational degree of freedom. We use CMB observations from SPT, Planck, and ACT, combined with DESI DR2 distance measurements, with and without the DESY5 Dovekie supernova sample. All three alternatives improve the best-fit likelihood relative to $\Lambda$CDM. When supernovae are included, the Akaike information criterion favors F42, while Ag and Qui remain nearly indistinguishable from $\Lambda$CDM on this criterion. The Bayesian evidence, however, does not establish a robust preference among the three alternatives. Our results show that improved fits to current observations can arise from physically different dark-energy histories, motivating complementary measurements of expansion and structure growth to distinguish them.

papers.title: The Sound of Dark Sectors in Pulsar Timing Arrays
papers.authors: Amitayus Banik, Yanou Cui, Yu-Dai Tsai, Yuhsin Tsai
papers.abstract: A phase transition in the dark sector (DS) presents a promising explanation for the stochastic gravitational wave (GW) signals detected in recent observations by Pulsar Timing Arrays (PTAs). Instead of focusing solely on fitting data with phenomenological parameters, we systematically delineate simple, underlying DS models at the microscopic, Lagrangian level and uncover the conditions required to yield the GW spectrum observed by PTAs. Within this framework, the characteristic scale of the dark sector is $O$(MeV), with complementary tests at future energy- and intensity-frontier experiments.

papers.title: The Synthetic Absorption Line Spectral Almanac (SALSA)
papers.authors: Dylan Nelson, Celine Peroux, Philipp Richter, Matthew M. Pieri, Sebastian Lopez, Rongmon Bordoloi, Siwei Zou, Joseph N. Burchett, Rebecca L. Davies, Rahul Ramesh, Matthew C. Smith, Sanchayeeta Borthakur, Christopher W. Churchill
papers.abstract: We create the first large-scale mock spectroscopic survey of gas absorption sightlines traversing the interstellar medium (ISM), circumgalactic medium (CGM), and intergalactic medium (IGM) surrounding galaxies of virtual Universes. That is, we create mock, or synthetic, absorption spectra by drawing lines-of-sight through cosmological hydrodynamical simulations, using a new mesh-free Voronoi ray-tracing algorithm. The result is the Synthetic Absorption Line Spectral Almanac (SALSA), which is publicly released on our online science platform. It spans a diverse range of ions, transitions, instruments, observational characteristics, modeling assumptions, redshifts, and numerical simulations. These include, but are not limited to: (ions) HI, OI, CI, MgI, MgII, FeII, SiII, CaII, ZnII, SiIII, SiIV, NV, CII, CIV, OVI; (instruments) SDSS-BOSS, KECK-HIRES, UVES, COS, DESI, 4MOST, WEAVE, XSHOOTER; (model choices) with/without dust depletion, noise, quasar continua, foregrounds; (redshift) from z=0 to z~6; (ancillary data) integrated equivalent widths, column densities, distances and properties of nearby galaxies; (simulations) IllustrisTNG including TNG50, TNG-Cluster, EAGLE, and SIMBA. We also provide Faraday rotation measure (RM) probing magnetic fields, and dispersion measure (DM) as traced by fast radio bursts (FRBs). The resulting dataset is generic and broadly applicable, enabling diverse science goals such as: (i) studies of the underlying physical gas structures giving rise to particular absorption signatures, (ii) galaxy-absorber and halo-absorber correlations, (iii) virtual surveys and survey strategy optimization, (iv) stacking experiments and the identification of weak absorption features, (v) assessment of data reduction methods and completeness calculations, (vi) inference of physical properties from observables, and (vii) apples-to-apples comparisons between simulations and data.

papers.title: Affine ANEC selects the closed FRW branch for geodesically complete cosmology
papers.authors: Nathan L. Burwig, Damien A. Easson
papers.abstract: Using the affinely parameterized averaged null energy condition (ANEC) along radial null geodesics, we prove that, within the globally nondegenerate Friedmann--Robertson--Walker (FRW) class with $a(t)>0$ for all cosmic times, non-static flat models and all open models cannot be both null geodesically complete and ANEC-satisfying. Bounded oscillatory or cyclic flat/open models obey the same obstruction; in non-static periodic cases the negative affine-ANEC contribution accumulates over infinitely many cycles, giving $I_{\rm ANEC}=-\infty$. The sign obstruction is absent in closed $(k=+1)$ FRW geometry, where positive curvature can offset the negative expansion contribution to the affine ANEC, allowing nonsingular, geodesically complete cosmologies with ordinary NEC-respecting matter. We construct closed-FRW scalar-field models and contrast them with their flat realizations, which require NEC-violating support. We show that neglecting small positive curvature in a flat reconstruction of the expansion history can produce an apparent phantom equation of state, with a percent-level shift at $z=1$. Our main result is a curvature classification of ANEC-compatible eternal FRW cosmologies within this class: non-static flat and all open models are obstructed, while the closed branch admits explicit complete realizations, with global de Sitter as the vacuum representative.

papers.title: Binary neutron stars in the next-generation era: multimessenger detection prospects and constraints on the equation of state, mass distribution, and cosmology
papers.authors: Hauke Koehn, Thibeau Wouters, Gilad Sadeh, Peter T.H. Pang, Mattia Bulla, Chris Van Den Broeck, Michael W. Coughlin, Tim Dietrich
papers.abstract: Next-generation gravitational-wave (GW) observatories will provide crucial insights into the nature of neutron star (NS) matter and the cosmological expansion history. We estimate the number of multimessenger detections of binary neutron stars (BNS) with the Einstein Telescope (ET) and Cosmic Explorer (CE) and project the resulting constraints on the equation of state (EOS), BNS mass distribution, and cosmology using joint hierarchical Bayesian inference. Our results rely on specific assumptions for the merger rate, EOS, and mass distribution; we consider two different mass functions, a narrow one centred around 1.4 $M_\odot$ and a wide one ranging from 1.1 to 2 $M_\odot$, and a merger rate with a local value of 107 Gpc$^{-3}$ yr$^{-1}$. Under this setup, our mock follow-up algorithm results in between $\sim40$ and $\sim100$ short-term electromagnetic counterparts per year for ET, depending on the detector layout and mass distribution. In a joint network with CE, this number ranges from $\sim 100$ to $\sim500$. Additionally, we project tens to hundreds of late-time afterglow detections from gamma-ray bursts or kilonovae (KNe). Based on the generated multimessenger events, we perform an injection campaign to hierarchically recover the EOS, mass distribution, and cosmology in a fully Bayesian framework. Focusing on KN events from ET alone, the multimessenger data from our largest analysed catalogue with 78 events can constrain the canonical NS radius $R_{1.4}$ to $\lesssim 0.2$ km and the Hubble constant $H_0$ to $\lesssim 1$ km s$^{-1}$ Mpc$^{-1}$, at least in absence of systematic modelling offsets. By comparing inference results that are solely based on GW data and those incorporating light-curve information, we find that while the latter has negligible impact on the EOS constraints, it can benefit the inference of cosmological parameters.

papers.title: Quasicrystalline Inflation: From the Cosmological Dipole to Primordial Diffraction
papers.authors: Jiro Soda
papers.abstract: We propose quasicrystalline inflation. Six quasiperiodic phases decompose into three phonons and three phasons. It turns out that a coherent pure-phason displacement can generate a local power dipole while the linear traceless quadrupole vanishes. From spatially varying quadratic effective field theory, we derive off-diagonal correlations whose momentum transfer is restricted to integer combinations of the six icosahedral wavevectors. These correlated off-diagonal signals provide a characteristic observational signature of primordial quasiperiodic order, primordial diffraction.
